essay:
# A reading both sides predicted settles nothing.

Two forecasters can watch the same number climb and both be right, because each of them predicted it. Most arguments about where AI goes next are like that: the evidence each side points to fits the other side's story too. For each question the outlook turns on, this page sets out what named writers argue, what each side expects this site's readings to show, what they show tonight, and, where this site has one, the reading that would tell the sides apart.

### Folio I · Can AI do whole jobs, reliably?

## Fast progress on single skills is what both sides expect; whole jobs are the test

The fastest story starts with a loop. Daniel Kokotajlo, who worked on governance at OpenAI, and his fellow forecasters at the AI Futures Project wrote AI 2027, a dated story in which each AI model, a program trained on text and data to write and reason, helps build the next, so progress feeds on itself until AI outdoes people at almost everything by the end of 2027 [cite:ai_2027]. They called 2027 their single most likely year rather than their middle estimate. They pushed their dates later at the end of 2025 and moved them earlier again in 2026, because coding agents, models set to carry out tasks on their own, had improved faster than they expected in late 2025 and early 2026 [cite:ai_futures_update]; their own check finds events running a little slower than the story [cite:ai_futures_q25].

Benjamin Jones, an economist at Northwestern who studies where growth and discoveries come from, answers with arithmetic. Research is a chain of steps and needs every one of them, so making some steps superhumanly fast leaves the rest, still slow, to set the pace, as a line of walkers moves at the speed of its slowest member. In his words, "bottlenecks severely mute the effect of extremely productive AI" [cite:jones_b]. What counts is the share of steps AI can take over.

Stephan Rabanser, Sayash Kapoor and their colleagues, Arvind Narayanan among them, computer scientists at Princeton who test AI agents, add that getting a task right is not getting it right every time: agents that solve more tasks each year still give different answers when the same task is run again, and agents must be dependable, not just accurate, before they are given work that matters [cite:agent_reliability]. Princeton's tracker of AI agents, which this site reads, scores each agent's accuracy and reliability from nought to one, and across the agents it has tested accuracy has risen by [fact:hal_accuracy_trend] and reliability by [fact:hal_reliability_trend], where a point is a hundredth of that range. AI 2027's story also has agents stumbling in their first years, so the gap settles nothing yet.

[plate:reliability]

The fastest clock settles nothing either. The length of the software tasks AI can finish doubles every [fact:horizon_doubling], at least as fast as AI 2027 assumed, but neither side doubts that single skills race ahead. Whole jobs separate them. On the Remote Labor Index, which scores models on real paid freelance projects completed end to end, the best model manages [fact:rli_record]. The compounding story, as written, needs most of those projects done by the end of 2027; the slowest-step story expects whole projects to trail single skills for years.

[plate:frontier]

### Folio II · Who checks the work?

## Whether checking AI's work becomes a business turns on who must answer for it

Markets run on knowing whom you are dealing with. Gillian Hadfield, who designs legal and regulatory systems for AI, and Andrew Koh, who studies how to design markets, point out that AI agents have none of the identity, registration or records that markets rely on, and sketch two routes, each with its own problems: tie each agent to a person or firm that answers for it, or give it legal standing and assets a court could seize [cite:hadfield_koh]. This site carries their argument one step further: if someone must answer for an agent's work, someone may be paid to check it. In February 2026 Gartner, which advises companies on what to buy, published a guide to the firms that sell platforms for testing and watching AI systems, and since January 2026 insurers have been able to attach optional standard wording that excludes harm from generative AI, the kind that writes and draws, from their general liability policies [cite:iso_exclusions]. The rival view is that the labs, the companies that build the most capable models, and the big cloud companies, which rent out computing, give checking away with their own platforms, and no reading yet tells the two apart.

Soren Larson, who writes about how money moves between the labs and the apps built on them and co-founded Crosshatch, a personalised-AI start-up that shut down in 2025, thinks apps that resell a lab's models by the token get squeezed. An app reselling a lab's model pays at least the lab's own price per token, the fragment of a word in which the use of a model is sold, and can charge little more than going to the lab directly would cost, so its margin, what is left of revenue after the cost of what was sold, shrinks towards whatever its own additions are worth [cite:larson_squeeze]. His argument rests on one observation: "To my knowledge labs do not offer special wholesale pricing" [cite:larson_squeeze]. Nobody publishes app margins, so it cannot be tested yet.

Platforms face the mirror image. Peyman Shahidi, John Horton and their colleagues, economists and a computer scientist who study online markets, one of whom, Andrey Fradkin, works for Amazon, argue that agents could slash the cost of searching and bargaining, and expect platforms to set rules for how outside agents may use them, much as websites tell search engines' crawlers, the programs that read the web for them, what they may read [cite:shahidi_etal]. Byrne Hobart and Nikhil Davar, who write The Diff, a newsletter on finance and technology, in an issue that discloses a holding in Amazon, read Amazon's blocking of Meta's shopping assistant in September 2026 as a sign that platforms gain enough from controlling their customers' dealings with AI to keep outside agents out [cite:hobart_inference]. Amazon had already gone to court in November 2025 to keep Perplexity's shopping agent off its site, while Etsy and Walmart agreed to let shoppers buy through OpenAI's chatbot. This site's hand-kept ledger for the past year puts fences at [fact:fences_ledger] and openings at [fact:openings_ledger], but it does not yet sweep both sides under one rule, so it tests nothing yet.

### Folio III · Is adoption slow, or just hard to see?

## Adoption at the pace of past technologies fits both stories, so the argument turns on what the statistics miss

Narayanan and Kapoor's larger argument is that AI is a normal technology, whose big effects on the economy will come over decades, at the pace at which people and institutions change how they work [cite:normal_tech]. The Census Bureau's survey of American businesses fits their account so far: [fact:firms_using_ai] of firms say they used AI somewhere in their business in the past two weeks, in line with the pace of past technologies rather than faster. History suggests the harder part comes after arrival. Diego Comin and Martí Mestieri, economists who study how technologies spread between countries, found that the delay before new technologies reach poor countries has narrowed towards rich countries', but that poor countries use them far less intensively, and that this gap in depth explains most of the widening of the income gap since 1820 [cite:comin_mestieri].

[plate:adoption]

Diane Coyle and John Lourenze Poquiz, economists at Cambridge who study how the economy is measured, reply that most use of AI is free and its gains come as better work and saved time, which the official statistics do not price, so measured output can lag, or even fall, while people are better off [cite:coyle_poquiz]. Set against ChatGPT's weekly users, OpenAI's paying subscribers come to [fact:paid_share]; the two are different counts, so this is not the share of users who pay, but it shows that most weekly users pay nothing. That fits both stories: people may not pay because the tool is not yet worth much, or because its value never passes through a till.

The clearest early sign may be in hiring. Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar and Ruyu Chen, economists at Stanford who study AI and work through payroll records, found that workers in their early twenties in the jobs most exposed to AI have fallen behind their less exposed peers, mostly because firms hire fewer of them [cite:canaries]. They describe the pattern without claiming to have proved its cause, so the comparison carries the weight. With each group's employment set at a hundred in November 2022, the young now stand at [fact:junior_gap] against workers over fifty in the most exposed fifth of jobs, and at [fact:junior_gap_control] in the least exposed. If the gap opened everywhere, something other than AI would be the likelier culprit.

### Folio IV · Does work reorganise fast enough to show up in output?

## Two economists have bet against an explosion, and tonight's reading is one both sides expected

The cleanest test here is a bet. Benjamin Moll, an economist at the London School of Economics who studies whole economies, and Alex Imas, a behavioural economist who leads the economics of advanced AI at Google DeepMind, on leave from Chicago Booth, are bullish on what AI will be able to do and still think growth of more than ten percent a year in the next decade or so extremely unlikely, since it would need several unlikely things at once, from fast automation across the economy to AI that automates research itself [cite:moll_imas]. In August 2026 they and five others took the other side of a bet from four people who bet, at odds of four to one against them, that in some quarter before 2034 American real output per person, output after inflation divided by the population, will stand [test:bet_fast_side] or more above the highest level it had reached a year or more before [cite:bet_fast_side]. Among the four is William MacAskill, a moral philosopher and senior research fellow at Forethought, a research group on advanced AI, who with Fin Moorhouse, then a researcher at Forethought and now at Google DeepMind, has argued that AI could compress a century of technological progress into a decade [cite:macaskill_moorhouse]. Tonight output per person stands [fact:gdp_pc_over_peak] above that level [cite:moll_imas_bet].

Charles Jones and Christopher Tonetti, economists at Stanford who study long-run growth, supply the slow side's arithmetic: work is a chain of tasks that substitute poorly for one another, so if AI follows the pattern of past automation, growth rises only slowly, to less than three percent a year even by 2075, while in their fastest calibration, in which machines everywhere improve as fast as they have in making computers, it passes seven percent by 2030, though even then output explodes only decades later [cite:jones_tonetti]. Nor would a fast path necessarily show early. Anton Korinek, Charles Jones and colleagues, economists who model growth under advanced AI, several of whom work for or advise Anthropic, turned assumptions about AI into paths for the economy, which they present as scenarios rather than forecasts, and found that "Across scenarios, almost all of the divergence comes after 2027" [cite:korinek_etal].

Even where AI works, the first thing it changes may not be hours. In 1930 John Maynard Keynes, whose work founded modern macroeconomics, suggested that within a century people might share out the little work left in a week of about fifteen hours [cite:keynes]. Betsey Stevenson, a labour economist at Michigan, expects the opposite order: the washing machine raised the standard of a clean house long before it shortened the hours spent on housework, and AI, she argues, will first raise how much people are expected to do [cite:stevenson].

The bet settles it by early 2034 at the latest. Output per person grew by [fact:gdp_pc_yoy] in the latest year, close to Jones and Tonetti's slow path [cite:jones_tonetti], though a reading like that fits the fastest of Korinek and colleagues' scenarios until about 2027 as well.

### Folio V · Who keeps the money?

## Whether the labs keep their margins turns on how fast open models catch up

Carlota Perez, an economist who studies technological revolutions and the financial bubbles that come with them, found the same sequence in each great surge of technology since 1771 that had run its course: a frenzy of investment that runs ahead of the uses, a crash, then a golden age in which the technology is put to work; writing in 2002, she placed the fifth, the information age, at the turning point after its crash [cite:perez]. The builders of the infrastructure rarely keep the value, note Arvind Narayanan and Akash Kapur, a senior fellow at New America who studies how AI is governed, with cloud computing and the leading chip foundry, a factory that makes chips for others, as partial exceptions. Selling access to the frontier models, the most capable ones, tends towards a commodity business, where buyers choose on price alone, so the labs' likeliest escape, they argue, is to move up the stack, into products and deployments built into their customers' work, where switching is costly [cite:nk_up_the_stack].

Hobart sets out when models become a commodity: once some labs give away open models, whose inner workings anyone may download and run, the marginal cost of serving the cheapest models comes down to the chips and power that run them, and a model has more pricing power where it is the best tool for a particular job [cite:hobart_round_trip] [cite:hobart_pacing]. Larson adds that even the best model need not be bid down, with a result from Simon Board and Marek Pycia, economists who study how sellers set prices over time. A monopolist selling something that lasts is usually forced to cut its price by buyers who wait for discounts; but if every buyer has another option, "the seller charges a constant price in every period equal to the monopoly price" [cite:board_pycia], the price it would charge if it could promise never to cut it, given what buyers can get elsewhere. For AI, the open model is the other option: the lab keeps charging for its lead and lets the buyers who will not pay go, though as open models close the gap its price and its market both shrink, and if they improve fast enough that buyers would rather wait for them, a pace he judges low, it is bid down after all [cite:larson_durability].

The readings so far fit both. Open models carry [fact:open_share] of the tokens routed to the busiest models on OpenRouter, a marketplace that passes developers' requests to many models, and trail the best closed ones by [fact:open_lag]. At list prices, among the open models that can be matched with a closed one as capable, the labs' own cheaper models even undercut them, costing a median [fact:open_premium] as much, though that is a single reading so far. Meanwhile NVIDIA and AMD take [fact:chips_gp_share] of the gross profit, revenue less the direct cost of what was sold, that they share with Microsoft's cloud arm and the estimates for OpenAI and Anthropic, the only cloud and lab figures this site can measure, and the biggest cloud and platform companies spend [fact:capex_to_revenue] as much a year on buildings and equipment as AI earns in revenue. David Cahn, an investor at Sequoia Capital, has raised, every year since 2023, his estimate of the revenue AI must eventually earn to pay back a year of that spending, though he now sees in AI's help with writing code a clearer way to earn it [cite:cahn_2026].

[plate:stack]

What the labs do with the best model's price while it still leads will settle it. If they cut it towards the open models' to keep its sales, Narayanan and Kapur's commodity view wins; if they keep a premium for the lead and let buyers go, Larson's does, though he expects even that premium to give way if open models improve fast enough that buyers wait for them.

### Where they agree

## A handful of points recur across these writers, and not only on one side

Selling access to a model that others can match, token by token, is a thin business; someone has to answer for what an AI agent does before it can be trusted with work that matters; checking AI's work becomes a costly task of its own; and people use AI well before firms reorganise around it. Where someone here dissents, the dissent is listed with the point.

[plate:whose]

### The futures still open

## Crossing progress with rules shows which futures tonight's readings still allow

How fast capability improves and how the rules on deploying AI settle will decide which future arrives. So far the rules have got lighter: the American president ordered moves against state AI laws in December 2025 [cite:eo_14365], Colorado replaced its AI Act with a narrower law on automated decisions in May 2026 [cite:colorado_sb26_189], and the European Union put off its rules for high-risk AI until the end of 2027 and beyond [cite:eu_2026_1744]. Kapoor and Narayanan had argued years earlier that licensing who may build models would not work [cite:nk_licensing].

The grid crosses the two and fills a cell only where a named writer argues it; a cell stays open while none of its signposts is failing its test, and every open cell is marked, never just one. What would close cells, and change the outlook: whole paid projects done end to end, labs cutting the best model's price or keeping a premium while it still leads, independent firms winning the checking, platforms fencing or opening, and output per person breaking away before 2030.

positions.mechanism: When everyone has the same models, what a firm knows about its own needs is its edge, and asking the market for help gives it away.
positions.title: Asking reveals what you want, so firms keep work inside

positions.case: Code that comes with tests is handed to AI before contracts that come with none.
positions.kill_shot: Work that is hard to check being handed over as fast as work that is easy to check.
positions.mechanism: A task is handed over when checking the result costs less than doing it. Hadfield and Koh argue about accountability; this site carries the argument to the order of adoption.
positions.title: What goes first is set by the cost of checking, not the cost of doing

positions.case: Moll and Imas expect AI's abilities to keep leaping and still think growth of four to five percent a year, which would itself be historic, is the more reasonable baseline [cite:moll_imas].
positions.kill_shot: A quarter before 2034 in which output per person clears the bet's line above the highest level it had reached a year or more before.
positions.mechanism: An explosion would need fast automation across the economy, spending that follows it, demand that absorbs the output, no cyberattacks by or with AI destroying value, and AI that automates research, all at once; and work is a chain of tasks that substitute poorly for one another, so AI that follows the pattern of past automation raises growth only slowly [cite:jones_tonetti].
positions.title: Growth rises, but does not explode

positions.case: MacAskill and three others have bet, at odds of four to one against them, on growth exploding before 2034 [cite:bet_fast_side], and in Korinek and colleagues' model a fast path looks like the others until about 2027 [cite:korinek_etal], so slow readings now do not count against it.
positions.kill_shot: AI's research effort rivalling humanity's without technological progress speeding up.
positions.mechanism: Once AI's thinking rivals the whole of humanity's, it keeps growing far faster than the number of people, research speeds up enormously and industry follows, so output can break away within a decade of AI matching human researchers.
positions.title: AI compresses a century of progress into a decade

positions.case: Appliances in the middle of the twentieth century raised standards of cleanliness long before they shortened the hours spent on housework.
positions.kill_shot: Paid hours in the most exposed work falling before output rises.
positions.mechanism: A tool that makes work easier first raises what people are expected to produce, as washing machines raised the standard of a clean house.
positions.title: Work gets more intense before it frees time

positions.case: If AI multiplies what an hour of work produces, the same needs can be met with fewer hours.
positions.kill_shot: Hours in the most exposed work rising as AI spreads.
positions.mechanism: As output per hour rises, people take part of the gain as leisure and share out the work that remains. Keynes argued it of machines in general in 1930; this site carries it to AI.
positions.title: Machines buy people time

positions.case: Richer households spend much more on care, teaching and hospitality.
positions.kill_shot: That work's share of spending and jobs falling as AI spreads.
positions.mechanism: As machines make other things cheap, spending moves to work where the person is part of what is bought.
positions.title: Work built on people dealing with people gains

positions.case: In Restrepo's model labour's share of income heads towards nothing once computing can do any work, even as total wages rise.
positions.kill_shot: Wages keeping pace with output as AI takes on more tasks.
positions.mechanism: Where better algorithms set the pace, wages jump and fall as tasks are automated [cite:restrepo]; where AI is sold with market power, Athey and Scott Morton add, workers can pay again when its price rises [cite:athey_scott_morton].
positions.title: Wages follow a jagged path, and the displaced can lose again

positions.case: Early evidence, by the authors' account, fits bigger firms and less local autonomy.
positions.kill_shot: Firms getting smaller and more decentralised as they adopt AI.
positions.mechanism: AI captures the local knowledge that used to justify leaving decisions to people on the spot.
positions.title: Decisions move to the centre

positions.case: The knowledge Hayek meant is local and fleeting and cannot be gathered into statistics; this site adds that a model trained on what is written may lack it.
positions.kill_shot: Firms that move decisions to the centre with AI outperforming those that leave them local.
positions.mechanism: What matters for most decisions is knowledge of particular times and places, which changes constantly and by its nature cannot reach the centre as statistics. Hayek argued it about central planning; this site carries it to AI.
positions.title: Knowledge on the spot keeps decisions there

positions.case: Cloudflare counts AI companies' crawlers, the programs that read websites for them, taking far more pages than they send visitors back, on news sites as elsewhere [cite:cloudflare_crawl], though it warns the count may be overstated where an app does not say where its visitors came from [cite:cloudflare_ratio].
positions.kill_shot: Visits to publishers from search and AI answers rising.
positions.mechanism: Sites that produce information are paid by visits, and AI that answers directly sends fewer of them.
positions.title: Answers replace visits, and the web that trained AI loses its income

positions.case: Cloudflare, which stands between many websites and their visitors, bought an AI data marketplace to build a system in which AI developers pay for the content they train on [cite:cloudflare_human_native].
positions.kill_shot: Publishers' income falling even where they charge AI companies.
positions.mechanism: As answers replace visits, publishers charge the AI companies directly, by licence or by the page.
positions.title: AI companies pay for what they read

positions.case: Open models trail the best closed ones by [fact:open_lag], months rather than years.
positions.kill_shot: Labs keeping a premium on models that open ones already match.
positions.mechanism: Where some labs give their models away, the marginal cost of serving the cheapest models comes down to the chips and power that run them, and a lab has more pricing power where its model is the best tool for the job.
positions.title: Tokens become a commodity where a model is not the best tool

positions.case: Near-frontier open models sell for a small fraction of the best model's price without, as Larson reads it, forcing the best model's price down.
positions.kill_shot: Labs cutting the best model's price to keep its sales while open models still improve too slowly for buyers to wait for them.
positions.mechanism: Buyers who will not pay a lab's price leave for an open model rather than wait for a discount, so the lab is not bid down to cost; it charges what its lead over the open alternative is worth and serves fewer buyers, and as open models close the gap its price and its market both shrink. Simon Board and Marek Pycia proved the first step for a monopolist selling a durable good whose buyers all have another option [cite:board_pycia].
positions.title: Labs charge for their lead and let buyers go

positions.case: Cloud computing escaped the same trap by becoming software, and the leading chip foundry by being almost alone.
positions.kill_shot: The labs' revenue staying mostly in selling access to their models by the token.
positions.mechanism: Selling access to a model tends towards a commodity business, so labs move into products and into deployments built into their customers' work, where switching is costly.
positions.title: Labs escape by moving up the stack, and lock their customers in

positions.case: Hobart reads the reports that Meta may use other firms' models for some of its answers this way.
positions.kill_shot: The owners of the best models taking users from the biggest platforms.
positions.mechanism: A platform with the most users gains most by serving good-enough models to all of them and selling better ones on top, whoever built them.
positions.title: The biggest platforms win with models that are good enough

positions.case: In Larson's own simulation, with the model held fixed, a harness trained on many firms' outcomes beat what each firm learned from its own, most of all on new kinds of problems.
positions.kill_shot: Firms learning as well from their own outcomes as a router does from everyone's.
positions.mechanism: A neutral router that pools many firms' checked outcomes learns to solve their problems, new kinds above all, faster than any one firm alone, and pricing by outcome belongs with it.
positions.title: Routers gain power

positions.case: This is the line in this site's essay on the migrating bottleneck, and Larson's argument contradicts it.
positions.kill_shot: Routers' share of traffic and their margins rising as models converge.
positions.mechanism: The better a router works, the more easily buyers move to the cheapest model that is good enough, the harder sellers compete on price, and the less anyone needs a router.
positions.title: A router works itself out of a job

positions.case: NVIDIA and AMD take [fact:chips_gp_share] of the gross profit they share with Microsoft's cloud arm and the estimates for OpenAI and Anthropic, the only cloud and lab figures this site can measure.
positions.kill_shot: The chip makers' share falling while chips stay scarce.
positions.mechanism: When every input is needed at once, the one hardest to get sets the pace and its owner takes the profit, until the industry builds its way out.
positions.title: Whoever holds the scarcest input collects

positions.case: The biggest cloud and platform companies spend [fact:capex_to_revenue] as much a year on buildings and equipment as AI earns in revenue.
positions.kill_shot: AI's revenue growing into the spending before the chips it bought are out of date.
positions.mechanism: The spending on data centres has to be paid back by revenue that has not arrived yet, and the chips it buys lose value fast, so if the revenue comes late the investors take the loss.
positions.title: The spending runs ahead of the revenue, and investors take the loss

positions.case: Cahn wrote in December 2025 that a few such delays had already been reported publicly.
positions.kill_shot: The new capacity coming online on schedule, with the price of computing falling as it arrives, the other outcome Cahn names.
positions.mechanism: Demand for computing runs into a supply chain that has not grown as fast, from the few firms that make the most advanced chips and the machines that make them to generators, cooling and skilled builders, so data centres are finished late while use keeps rising.
positions.title: The build-out runs late while use keeps rising

positions.case: Sundheim, whose firm holds stakes in OpenAI and Anthropic, points to the labs' coding tools and the paid access to their models as businesses customers stick with.
positions.kill_shot: Customers switching between models freely on price, or more than a handful of labs staying at the frontier.
positions.mechanism: Customers could switch between models as easily as between clouds but mostly do not, and staying at the frontier costs too much capital for more than a handful of labs.
positions.title: The labs are durable businesses with high margins

positions.case: Across American nonfarm business from 1948 to 2001, innovators kept, by his central estimate, about two cents of each dollar of value they created [cite:nordhaus].
positions.kill_shot: AI firms' profits growing as fast as the value their users get.
positions.mechanism: Competition and imitation pass most of an innovation's value to the people who use it, through lower prices; the innovators keep a sliver. Nordhaus measured it across American nonfarm business from 1948 to 2001; this site carries it to AI.
positions.title: Consumers keep most of the value

positions.case: Open models a few steps behind the best keep getting better, and each release widens what a device can do on its own.
positions.kill_shot: Everyday use staying in cloud data centres even as capable open models shrink.
positions.mechanism: Once a small model on a phone or laptop is good enough, running it there is cheaper and faster than paying a data centre for each request, and the meter stops.
positions.title: AI's everyday work moves onto people's own devices

positions.case: Almost all paid use today runs through the labs' and clouds' own services.
positions.kill_shot: A large share of everyday requests answered on the device.
positions.mechanism: The best models stay too large for a device, and people want the best model for work that matters.
positions.title: The cloud keeps the thinking

positions.case: In June 2026 the United States required one leading developer to hold a licence before any foreign national could use its most advanced models, and they were withdrawn worldwide [cite:woodward_rogoyski]. The consultancy's writers report that each of the two states' leading models are unavailable to customers in the other, or under growing political scrutiny there [cite:bcg_great_divide].
positions.kill_shot: The same leading models being sold on the same terms in every large market, with no rule standing between a firm and the model it would choose.
positions.mechanism: The most capable models are made by a few firms in two states, and each state can license, limit or withdraw what those firms sell abroad, so a buyer's choice of model is bounded by where it sits.
positions.title: Governments decide which countries and firms may use which models

positions.case: Open models trail the best closed ones by [fact:open_lag], months rather than years, and most of China's leading models are published for anyone to run [cite:bcg_great_divide].
positions.kill_shot: Open models falling far enough behind, or being restricted themselves, that a firm shut out of the closed ones has nothing comparable to run.
positions.mechanism: A model whose maker publishes it can be copied and run anywhere, so a rule on who may buy a closed model leaves a capable open one within everyone's reach; the writers who argue the other side themselves name open models as the hedge.
positions.title: Open models cross borders, so access cannot be fenced

positions.case: The labs are turning from staged practice tasks towards records of real work, and pay for access to them.
positions.kill_shot: Staged practice tasks going on improving models at long, hard-to-check office work.
positions.mechanism: Practice tasks written by outside contractors cannot teach a model long work whose results are hard to check, in fields such as biology and security; only records of how experts actually do that work can.
positions.title: Training data comes from real work inside firms

positions.case: Labs are buying records from an airline and from start-ups that have wound down, and the gains may spill into neighbouring fields.
positions.kill_shot: The labs staying interchangeable in every industry, with none ahead in a trade because of the data it bought.
positions.mechanism: The labs' general skills converge, so what separates them is the specialist business records each has bought, and each grows strongest in the trades it bought most from.
positions.title: Labs may pull apart by industry, on the records they buy

positions.case: Sellers focused on one field keep winning lab budgets from the large all-purpose vendors.
positions.kill_shot: One or two sellers coming to handle most of what the frontier labs buy.
positions.mechanism: Each field and each kind of data needs its own experts and its own checks, so no one seller can be best at all of them.
positions.title: The data market stays split among specialists

positions.case: Recruiting, checking and security reviews may cost less per task the larger the seller.
positions.kill_shot: Specialist sellers taking a growing share of the labs' data budgets.
positions.mechanism: Labs want one supplier that can recruit experts at volume, check quality and pass security reviews, and those costs favour the largest sellers.
positions.title: A few large sellers take most of the data market

positions.case: Firms want models fitted to their own work and run where they control them, and open models are good enough to start from.
positions.kill_shot: These firms staying in separate businesses rather than converging on selling tuned models by use.
positions.mechanism: Hosting models, selling data and custom training each lead to the same product, an open model fitted to a firm's own work and billed by use.
positions.title: Tuning open models for firms becomes one business

positions.case: Cai expects the gains from custom training to be nearly wiped out by each general release, outside regulated niches where data is scarce.
positions.kill_shot: Models built for one field keeping their lead over each new general release.
positions.mechanism: Each new general model from the labs learns many fields at once, so a model trained for one field keeps its edge only until the next release.
positions.title: General models overtake models built for one field

positions.case: Agents working in parallel multiply what a model can finish, at a price.
positions.kill_shot: Valuable office tasks staying out of AI's reach even where computing is cheap.
positions.mechanism: Once many agents can work on a task at once, what limits the work is the cost of the computing and the systems around it, not what a single model can do.
positions.title: Cost, not ability, becomes the limit

positions.case: Labs, investors and software firms all compete for these engineers, and labs buy the consultancies that employ them.
positions.kill_shot: These roles becoming easy to fill, and their pay premium fading.
positions.mechanism: Every firm's work is different, and fitting a model to it takes engineers who understand both the model and the firm, of whom there are few.
positions.title: Engineers who fit AI to each firm are the scarce ingredient

positions.case: Chinese labs release strong open models, yet the best closed models from American labs have stayed ahead of them.
positions.kill_shot: A Chinese lab's model becoming the best at the frontier.
positions.mechanism: The tests that define the frontier, the work it is judged on and the customers who pay are mostly American, and the most advanced chips stay hard for Chinese labs to get.
positions.title: Chinese labs do not take the lead

positions.case: Rival labs are close enough that a customer's cost of switching between them stays small.
positions.kill_shot: Customers becoming bound to one lab by exclusive deals and bans on copying.
positions.mechanism: Competition among the frontier labs keeps switching cheap, and bans on copying models and exclusive deals leak.
positions.title: Labs cannot lock their customers in

positions.case: A system built from several models needs each to fit its part.
positions.kill_shot: Buyers treating models as interchangeable and choosing on the price of a token alone.
positions.mechanism: Models differ in efficiency and in the kinds of input they handle, and a system built from several models needs each one to fit its part.
positions.title: Models stay different, not interchangeable

positions.case: Adding capacity means new buildings, power and chips, none of which can be added at once.
positions.kill_shot: A sudden glut sending the rent for AI chips down by most of its value within a year.
positions.mechanism: New capacity takes years to plan, power and build, so it cannot be multiplied overnight the way new fibre equipment multiplied internet bandwidth.
positions.title: Computing cannot flood the market overnight

positions.case: Each shortage draws investment, and some suppliers respond faster than expected.
positions.kill_shot: Every part squeezed by AI's demand staying scarce and rising in price.
positions.mechanism: AI's demand strains every link from memory to power at once; somewhere supply will prove easier to expand than expected, and prices there will turn.
positions.title: Some link in the chip chain proves easier to expand

positions.case: The largest technology firms already pay to train electricians and other tradespeople.
positions.kill_shot: Data centres being finished on time once the money is committed.
positions.mechanism: A data centre can be financed and designed quickly, but the grid is planned for slow change with warning, and electricians and welders are few; neither can be hurried.
positions.title: The grid and tradespeople set the pace of building

positions.case: The title of best model has already passed between labs several times.
positions.kill_shot: One lab keeping the best model for several years running.
positions.mechanism: The lab with the most popular model spends its chips serving it, leaving less to train the next, while rivals with spare chips train theirs.
positions.title: The lead among labs keeps changing hands

positions.case: Labs have already gated models they judged too capable to publish at once.
positions.kill_shot: Labs releasing their best models to the public as soon as they are trained.
positions.mechanism: No government agrees a pause, but the largest labs, loosely in step, slow the public release of their most powerful models.
positions.title: Labs hold back their strongest models

positions.case: Every lab that waits hands its customers to a rival that does not.
positions.kill_shot: Labs keeping their best models back from the public.
positions.mechanism: Labs compete for users and revenue, so a model kept back is revenue handed to a rival.
positions.title: The best models go to everyone at once

positions.case: Hobart expects labs to buy operating firms in the trades they serve, gaining customers and assets that can answer for mistakes.
positions.kill_shot: Buyers taking AI's work on long, unpredictable tasks from parties that cannot answer for its mistakes.
positions.mechanism: When an agent does long, unpredictable work, the buyer wants someone with assets and a licence who answers for its mistakes, so AI reaches customers through such parties.
positions.title: AI's work is bought through firms that can be sued

positions.case: Start-ups take [fact:startup_app_share] of what American firms spend on AI apps, by Menlo Ventures' survey, though the survey leaves out AI built into incumbents' existing software.
positions.kill_shot: Established firms taking most of what firms spend on AI apps.
positions.mechanism: Start-ups built around AI are cheaper and faster, and contracts and insurance can carry the liability.
positions.title: Firms buy AI straight from the start-ups that build it

positions.case: Ramp, which handles firms' card spending, counts their median AI spending per employee at [fact:ramp_spend], up on a year before.
positions.kill_shot: Firms' AI spending levelling off or falling while prices keep dropping.
positions.mechanism: Each fall in price makes AI worth using for more work, and use grows faster than the price falls.
positions.title: Firms' AI bills keep rising as prices fall

positions.case: Each generation of models does last year's work for a fraction of the price.
positions.kill_shot: Firms' spending on AI per employee rising year after year.
positions.mechanism: Work gets moved to cheaper models and fixed routines, so falling prices cut the bill faster than new uses add to it.
positions.title: Firms' AI spending levels off as prices fall

positions.case: AI's use keeps growing while the public grows warier of it.
positions.kill_shot: Public approval of AI rising clearly and politicians campaigning in its favour.
positions.mechanism: Most of AI's benefits are hard to see, while those facing automation outnumber those doing it, so politicians gain by opposing it.
positions.title: AI grows unpopular, and its rules come late

positions.case: Rules for a technology often come from agencies, courts and standards bodies long before voters take it up.
positions.kill_shot: AI becoming a central issue in national elections.
positions.mechanism: Agencies, courts and industry standards set AI's rules before it becomes a voting issue.
positions.title: AI's rules are settled quietly

positions.case: Labs and data sellers already pay experts to set down how they do their work.
positions.kill_shot: Few occupations showing workers shifting to producing training data.
positions.mechanism: The fastest way to teach a model a job is to record people doing it, so in some jobs the work becomes producing that record.
positions.title: Some workers turn into trainers of their replacements

positions.case: NVIDIA has invested in cloud companies that rent out its chips and in labs that buy them.
positions.kill_shot: NVIDIA's revenue staying almost wholly one-off sales of hardware.
positions.mechanism: NVIDIA lends to and invests in the data centres that buy its chips in return for a share of their income, turning one-off sales into a stream and gaining a say over who gets capacity.
positions.title: NVIDIA finances its customers

positions.case: Labs and clouds already buy capacity from one another in every direction.
positions.kill_shot: The largest firms keeping their computing for their own use and renting none of it out.
positions.mechanism: The largest technology firms build more computing than they need and rent the spare to rivals, turning each firm's bet into one bet, shared across the industry, that demand for AI keeps growing.
positions.title: The builders overbuild and rent out the rest

positions.case: Search shows how much advertisers pay for a clear sign of what someone wants; assistants can see that want earlier.
positions.kill_shot: Ads in assistants driving users away or earning far less per user than ads in search.
positions.mechanism: Assistants can see what people want to buy earlier than search does, so advertisers will pay to reach them, and ads fund the free versions.
positions.title: Advertising pays for free AI

positions.case: Firms build more of their own software with coding agents while still running on the same systems of record.
positions.kill_shot: Software that holds a business's records losing customers as fast as other software.
positions.mechanism: Coding agents let firms build their own tools instead of buying them, but the programs that hold a business's core records are hard to replace and every new tool needs them.
positions.title: The software that keeps the records gains

positions.case: The labs keep adding engineers who work inside customers' firms.
positions.kill_shot: Labs reporting gross margins as high as software firms' while running large teams inside their customers.
positions.mechanism: Labs need staff inside their customers to deploy their models, and that staff grows with the customers.
positions.title: Deployment staff pull the labs' margins down

positions.case: Firms buy AI for any task where it returns more than it costs, however small.
positions.kill_shot: New businesses in small information niches not rising as AI's costs fall.
positions.mechanism: Once a task costs less by machine than any worker would, services appear that were never worth paying a person for, and growth comes from filling them.
positions.title: Cheap AI fills niches no one served

positions.case: Firms building around AI hire for range more than for depth.
positions.kill_shot: Specialists keeping their value over versatile workers.
positions.mechanism: When AI does the specialised steps, the valuable worker is the one who can direct it across many of them.
positions.title: Versatile workers pull ahead of specialists

positions.case: Walker sets his prediction explicitly against the view that AI makes every firm bigger.
positions.kill_shot: Firms growing larger across AI-exposed industries, applications included.
positions.mechanism: Codifying a firm's knowledge for AI is costly, lossy and needs upkeep, so scale pays where the work is generic, in computing and models, while firms closest to a trade's own knowledge win in applications.
positions.title: Big at the base, small at the top

positions.case: Hoffman points to founders folding their companies into AI-run groups and to industrial chiefs who say the old case for scale has run out.
positions.kill_shot: AI-run groups trading below the sum of their parts, as conglomerates did.
positions.mechanism: AI lets one centre see and run many unrelated businesses, removing the overhead that made conglomerates trade at a discount.
positions.title: The conglomerate comes back

positions.case: NVIDIA and AMD take [fact:chips_gp_share] of the gross profit (sales minus the direct cost of making them) that this site can measure across chips, one cloud and the leading labs; that share is up on the year, though it slipped in the latest quarter. Yet chips from other designers already make up [fact:silicon_share_now] of the AI computing shipped so far, including custom chips that Broadcom and others build for large cloud and model companies. TSMC's filing calls its scale and capacity, particularly for advanced processes (the newest generations of chip-making, which print the smallest features), a major competitive advantage, and its biggest customers as a group have taken a larger part of its revenue each year since 2023, even as its single largest customer's share fell. ASML says it is currently the world's only maker of extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines, which print the finest features with light of a very short wavelength, and that one supplier, Carl Zeiss, makes all their optics and limits how many it can build. Against this unit, this site reads foundry supply as easing: TSMC's capacity is catching up with demand. That undercuts the title's claim for the foundry only if the easing reaches TSMC's own prices and margins, which this site cannot yet see, since TSMC files under international accounting rules this site's filing reader does not read. The three designers' own conditions do not collide: NVIDIA's, Broadcom's and AMD's can all hold at once until chips from other designers make up most of the AI computing shipped.
positions.commoditising: Chips made on older processes are cheap and interchangeable; TSMC's own filing says rivals in those processes are numerous. This site judges that the cost of a unit of computing keeps falling with each chip generation, and that the general-purpose AI chip is being copied from below: every large buyer that designs its own chip, often with Broadcom's help, turns part of NVIDIA's market into a price to negotiate. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers as lower prices and better products.
positions.converts_if: For the designer: its software (for NVIDIA, CUDA, the platform developers write AI code against) and its whole-rack systems with their own links between chips keep buyers even when rival chips are plentiful and cheaper, turning a shortage rent into switching costs, what a customer would lose by moving to a rival. For the foundry and the toolmaker: they keep a lead at each new process, so their scale and process power outlive the AI shortage.
positions.kill_shot: NVIDIA keeping both its share of AI chip supply and its gross margin while AMD's chips and the custom chips ship in volume and wafer supply at the newest processes keeps growing fast; or a second foundry making AI chips at the newest process in volume for a major designer.
positions.mechanism: Three kinds of firm make AI chips. Designers such as NVIDIA, AMD and Broadcom draw them; a foundry (a factory that makes chips to other firms' designs), above all TSMC, prints them onto wafers (thin discs of silicon, each later cut into many chips); and toolmakers such as ASML build the machines that do the printing. Eliyahu Goldratt, a physicist who studied factories, found that a system runs at the pace of its slowest part. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. So while buyers cannot get enough chips, the designer they most want takes the rent. This site judges that as more chips arrive and the biggest buyers design their own, that rent is exposed, while the foundry and the toolmaker keep theirs for as long as no rival can match what they do.
positions.stays_scarce: This site judges that capacity at the newest processes, and the machines that print it, stay scarce. A new factory for the newest process takes years to build and the skill to run it takes longer. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier, and named the kinds that recur. Two apply here: process power (a way of working that takes rivals years to learn) and scale economies (unit costs that fall as volume grows, so a rival must match the volume to match the cost). The EUV machines have one maker, fed by one optics supplier: a cornered resource, Helmer's term for preferential access to something others need, which does not ease when chips do.
positions.title: The chip designer's lead is a shortage profit; the foundry's and the toolmaker's are harder to copy

positions.case: SK hynix reported record results for 2025, with HBM revenue growing sharply and demand for ordinary server memory rising sharply too. Samsung describes low inventory and supply constraints in memory. This site's tightness word for memory reads moderate, though memory is counted in dollars, so a price rise looks like more memory. Micron's own filing warns that if HBM demand weakens and makers shift capacity back to ordinary DRAM, its supply could rise sharply, and that an oversupplied market pushes prices down; it also names Chinese state-backed makers, CXMT and YMTC, among the causes of that risk.
positions.commoditising: Ordinary memory, the kind in phones and laptops, is a textbook commodity: identical parts, several makers, and prices that swing with each wave of new factories. Networking built to open standards such as Ethernet, which Broadcom sells to the largest cloud and model companies, is interchangeable by design. Eliyahu Goldratt, a physicist who studied factories, found that a system runs at the pace of its slowest part, and David Ricardo, an English economist who studied why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. On their account the rent in memory lasts only until the makers build their way out, and SK hynix says it is building new factories in Korea.
positions.converts_if: Custom HBM, memory built to one buyer's design, which SK hynix calls a key differentiator, becomes the norm, so each chip generation is locked to one maker and switching costs replace the shortage. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than rivals, named switching costs, what a customer would lose by moving to a rival, as one of the lasting advantages he found. In networking, the rent lasts only if NVIDIA's own links stay faster than open standards by enough that buyers accept being tied to one vendor.
positions.kill_shot: Memory makers keeping record margins through a year in which all three add HBM capacity faster than AI chip shipments grow and ordinary memory prices fall.
positions.mechanism: An AI chip is only as fast as the memory that feeds it. High-bandwidth memory, or HBM, is DRAM (the working memory a processor reads and writes constantly) cut into dies (single chips), stacked and placed beside the processor so data reaches it quickly. This site counts three makers: SK hynix, Samsung and Micron. Micron's filing says HBM needs more wafers (the silicon discs chips are cut from) and more factory space than ordinary DRAM for the same amount of memory, so when AI demand runs ahead the makers profit, and if it weakens they can turn the same factories back to ordinary memory. Networking, the switches, cables and light-based links that join many chips into one machine, splits in two: NVIDIA's own links, which tie buyers to its systems, and gear built to open standards, which any maker can supply.
positions.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is the skill to stack dies with good yield (the share of units that work) and to be qualified (tested and approved) by a chip designer for its next product; a newcomer would need both, and this site judges they take longer to learn than one product generation. NVIDIA's own links between chips stay scarce because only NVIDIA makes them, though its filing says it now lets other firms' chips connect to them.
positions.title: High-bandwidth memory is a cyclical commodity earning a shortage's price

positions.case: This site reads electricity as severe and data-centre buildings as tight, though the electricity reading measures only how fast demand grows, not supply. The biggest cloud and platform companies spend [fact:capex_to_revenue] as much a year on buildings and equipment as AI earns in revenue, so money is not what is short; this site reads capital as slack. TSMC's filing names constraints in power supply among the things that could slow demand for its chips. Against this unit, power generated on site beside the data centre, and chips that do more work for each unit of electricity, would both loosen the grid's hold. The wait to be connected is the gauge that would show the shortage directly, and this site knows of no public series for it.
positions.commoditising: This site judges that the building itself, the shell, the racks and much of the cooling, follows standard designs that many contractors can put up, and that money for the build-out is plentiful. David Teece, an economist who studied why the firm that invents something often fails to keep the returns, called the inputs an innovation needs to reach its customers complementary assets; generic ones, which anyone can buy, earn an ordinary return, not a rent.
positions.converts_if: Holders of connected sites and running power stations lock their buyers into long contracts at prices set during the shortage, or regulators let utilities earn a guaranteed return on new lines built for data centres, turning a shortage rent into a regulated one. It fails to convert if power built on site, beside the data centre and off the grid, proves quick and cheap.
positions.kill_shot: New large sites being connected to the grid about as fast as they are built, with the rent for powered data-centre space falling while use keeps rising.
positions.mechanism: A data centre needs three things: a building, money, and electricity delivered through a grid connection. This site judges that buildings and money can be had quickly, while a new connection means waiting for the utility to add lines and transformers, and new power stations take years. Eliyahu Goldratt, a physicist who studied factories, found that a system runs at the pace of its slowest part; David Ricardo, an English economist who studied why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. So, in this site's judgement, the rent goes to whoever already holds land with power and a connection. Much of that input sits with utilities whose prices a regulator sets, so they cannot charge what the shortage is worth; this site judges that the rent leaks instead to owners of connected sites and of power stations already running.
positions.stays_scarce: This site judges that grid connections, heavy electrical gear such as large transformers and turbines, and the electricians and other trades who install them stay scarce. A connection is close to a licence: a utility grants it under a regulator's rules and it cannot be copied, which makes it what Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied lasting advantages, calls a cornered resource: preferential access to something others need. Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, and Oliver Williamson, who studied contracts and found that a buyer who depends on an asset built for it can be squeezed by whoever owns it, would expect the largest buyers to own such assets or lock them up in long contracts.
positions.title: A site already wired to the grid is scarcer than the building or the money

positions.case: The big clouds' own segment profits are high: this site's filed figures show AWS, Google Cloud and Microsoft's cloud segment each earning a high operating margin (profit after running costs, as a share of sales), one that moves up and down from quarter to quarter. Oracle's filing says some of its cloud offerings are concentrated among a number of large customers, and that some customers may be heavily in debt. Their spending runs far ahead of AI's revenue: the biggest cloud and platform companies spend [fact:capex_to_revenue] as much a year on buildings and equipment as AI earns in revenue. Microsoft's remaining performance obligations (revenue customers have signed for but not yet received) stand at [fact:msft_backlog] its revenue over the past year, against [fact:msft_backlog_year_ago] a year before. The clouds also fund their own customers: Microsoft's filing calls it a major investor in OpenAI with rights to OpenAI's models, and Amazon's filing records investments in Anthropic and a large gain on them in 2025. Microsoft warns that overestimating demand could leave its data centres underused and force it to write down their value (cut the value it records for them). Amazon lengthened the working life it assumes for its servers in 2024, then shortened it for some servers and network equipment in 2025, citing how fast AI technology moves. Oracle set up a programme to sell new shares into the market over time, but had sold none by the end of May 2026. On the neocloud side, CoreWeave's filing says its largest customer, Microsoft, gave it most of its revenue in 2025, that OpenAI and Meta have signed large contracts, that customers commit to take-or-pay contracts (they pay for the capacity whether or not they use it), and that it finances its infrastructure mainly with debt secured on those contracts. Nebius says the long contracts it signed with Microsoft and Meta came with financing terms that let it grow, while most of its customer contracts so far have been short. The hourly rent for NVIDIA's previous-generation flagship chip changed by [fact:h100_rent_yoy] over the past year on this site's latest reading (a minus sign would mark a fall).
positions.commoditising: This site judges that an hour on a given GPU is becoming a commodity: the same NVIDIA chips are rented by many firms, Nebius names CoreWeave, Crusoe and Lambda as well as the big clouds among its rivals, and CoreWeave says its customers specify NVIDIA's chips, so the chip, not the cloud, is what they are buying. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers as lower prices. On that finding, the rent on each generation of chips falls towards cost as those chips become plentiful. David Teece, an economist who studied why the firm that invents something often fails to keep the returns, called the inputs a product needs to reach its customers complementary assets. This site judges that a neocloud's rack of rented chips is a generic one, which anyone with money, power and a supply of chips can assemble; the scarce inputs behind it belong to others, NVIDIA's chips on one side and the demand of a few big buyers on the other.
positions.converts_if: The big clouds turn chip rental into services customers build on, such as their own chips, their own model catalogues and the tools that run AI inside a firm's data, so switching costs hold AI work as they hold older work. For a neocloud: long take-or-pay contracts with buyers who can pay, signed during the shortage, outlast it, and it wins powered sites others cannot get, a cornered resource in Helmer's term (preferential access to something others need). Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, and Oliver Williamson, who found that a buyer that depends on an asset built for it can be squeezed by its owner, would expect the biggest buyers to build their own capacity once they can, which is the risk a neocloud's contracts must outlast.
positions.kill_shot: Big-cloud margins falling to the neoclouds' level as AI becomes most of what they sell, with customers moving AI work between clouds on price alone; or a neocloud keeping its margin through a year in which GPU rents fall steeply and its largest customer leaves at the end of its contract.
positions.mechanism: A cloud rents out computing by the hour or by the contract. The big clouds, often called hyperscalers (Microsoft's Azure, Amazon's AWS, Google Cloud and Oracle), sell AI chips alongside storage, databases and the software businesses already run on them. The neoclouds (newer firms such as CoreWeave, Nebius, Crusoe, Lambda and Fluidstack that rent out mostly NVIDIA's graphics chips, GPUs, and little else) sell the chips almost alone. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. This site judges that a neocloud's margin is that kind of rent, the gap between what a scarce chip rents for and what it costs to buy, power and borrow against, and that it lasts while chips and powered buildings are short; a big cloud's margin rests more on customers whose data and systems already sit inside it.
positions.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is powered, connected data-centre space and, for the big clouds, the customer relationships and the data already stored with them. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier. Scale economies and switching costs apply to the big clouds' existing business today: scale economies (unit costs that fall as volume grows, so a rival must match the volume to match the cost; Google offers its own AI chips, TPUs, beside GPUs) and switching costs (what a customer would lose by moving to a rival, here the work of moving data and systems built around one cloud). This site judges that neither is yet proven for AI work in particular, which is younger and easier to move than the systems firms have run in the cloud for years.
positions.title: The big clouds keep a rent from customers who stay; the neoclouds earn the shortage's price on borrowed money

positions.case: Open models trail the best closed ones by [fact:open_lag] on this site's latest reading, and on OpenRouter, a service that routes developers' requests to many models, open models took [fact:open_share] of the tokens among its most used models. The price of a given level of capability falls steeply on the estimate of Epoch, a research group that tracks AI, which this site reads as emerging. Against that, the businesses paying for AI, on the card and bill-payment data of Ramp, a firm that handles companies' spending, are concentrated among few labs, while the developers routing through OpenRouter spread their tokens across many more labs. The labs spend far ahead of their revenue: for OpenAI and Anthropic, a year of revenue at the current pace is well below the equity (money investors paid for shares) each has raised, and this site's last reading for xAI, taken before its merger into SpaceX, was also well below. Those revenue figures come mostly from the labs themselves, and investors value the labs at many times that revenue. The labs are buying their way up the stack, into the layers above them that sit closer to users: this site's acquisition ledger counts [fact:lab_deals_now] deals in the past year by which model and computing firms took companies in the layers above, including OpenAI's purchases of consumer apps and of a firm that installs AI inside companies, and Anthropic's of developer tools. Some labs already reach users directly: Google puts its Gemini model into Search and its apps, OpenAI reaches consumers through ChatGPT, its chat app, and Microsoft, which is not a frontier lab on this site's map, holds rights to OpenAI's models for its own products and has a revenue-share agreement with OpenAI. The strongest case against this site's judgement comes from Giovanni Cattani, an investor at Hummingbird Ventures, a venture capital firm, and before that an analyst at Blackstone, a private-investment firm. In an article he published on X, the social network, in early September 2026, titled 'Nobody is talking seriously about AI demand', he argued that the frontier labs' revenue rests on a few open-ended, long tasks, such as AI research, writing software and trading, where buyers always want the best model and will pay the labs' margins; on work with a natural limit, he argued, cheaper models from outside the frontier, firms that run models for others, and small models tuned to one job win instead. On that view the rent holds for as long as the uses of AI keep spreading into open-ended work.
positions.commoditising: This site judges that answering a well-understood request, the kind a model from a year before could already handle, is a commodity: many labs and open models do it, and it is priced close to the cost of the chips and power that run it. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers as lower prices and better products. Kenneth Arrow, an economist who studied how markets handle knowledge, argued that information is hard to own because copying it is cheap; a model's behaviour can be observed and partly copied by a rival training on its answers.
positions.converts_if: Labs turn deployments into switching costs: their coding agents, business tools and staff inside customers become part of how firms work, so moving to a rival means rebuilding, not just repointing. Or a lab owns the place users meet AI, as a chat app with a habit behind it, which Helmer would call branding (a buyer pays more for the same thing because of its name) or network economies (the product grows more useful as more people use it). David Teece, an economist who studied why inventors often fail to keep the returns from what they invent, found that the firm holding the complementary assets (the distribution, sales and systems a product needs to reach buyers) often keeps the profit; Google and Meta already hold theirs, and OpenAI and Anthropic are buying theirs. The rent also lasts, without either, if open-ended uses where only the best model will do keep growing faster than bounded ones, the case Giovanni Cattani makes above. Rules could entrench it too: Sayash Kapoor and Arvind Narayanan, computer scientists at Princeton who study what AI can and cannot do, argued that licensing who may build models, combined with limits on sharing them, would leave only a handful of firms able to build the most capable ones; this site reads that as a route to a regulatory rent (a profit protected by a licence rivals cannot get), which would make the lead last.
positions.kill_shot: Labs keeping their price premium and their share of business spending on models that open ones already match, with no growth in deployments or products; or, the other way, business spending spreading across many labs and open models as freely as developers' routed tokens already do.
positions.mechanism: The frontier labs, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, xAI and Meta, train the most capable AI models: programs trained on huge amounts of text and data to write, reason and carry out tasks. They sell their use by the token (a fragment of a word) and through products such as chat apps and coding tools. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. Today the scarce input is the best model, and the lab that has it charges for it. This site judges that the rent on a lead is transitional, because open-weight models (whose trained settings, the weights, are published for anyone to run) arrive some months behind, and that it becomes durable only where a lab is woven into how its customers work or owns the place where users meet it.
positions.stays_scarce: This site judges that the newest model at the frontier stays scarce for as long as it leads, and that training one costs so much in chips and money that only a handful of firms attempt it. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier; the one that clearly applies today is scale economies (the cost of training a model is fixed, so a lab with more users spreads it thinner, and a rival must match the users to match the cost). Switching costs (what a customer would lose by moving to a rival) are emerging, not proven: they exist where a lab's tools are built into a firm's systems, but this site cannot yet measure how often firms use several labs at once, so it does not count them in this group's powers.
positions.title: A frontier lab's lead earns a rent that open models chase within months; it lasts only where the lab is built into its customers' work

positions.case: This site has revenue readings for few of the neolabs. The voice specialist ElevenLabs reports a run-rate (a recent month's revenue scaled up to a year) that rose fast from the end of 2025 to April 2026 and more slowly since, evidence that a specialist off the big labs' path can earn money. For Mistral, a year of revenue at the current pace is well below the equity it has raised, though that gap has narrowed during 2026. The frontier labs' own costs are the hurdle: training at the frontier costs so much that, on this site's reading, even the leading labs' revenue is well below what they have raised. The specialists face a different test: open models trail the best closed ones by only [fact:open_lag], so a new lab's lead in a general model is short-lived, while a specialty in voice, video, robots or science may lie outside what the general labs train for. This site's acquisition ledger counts only purchases of firms in the layers above the models, so it cannot show a neolab being bought, or its leaders hired, by a bigger lab. This site judges which neolabs sit off the big labs' path; it does not measure it.
positions.commoditising: This site judges that a general model from a new lab is commoditising fastest of all: it competes with the frontier labs above it and the open-weight labs below it. Kenneth Arrow, an economist who studied how markets handle knowledge, argued that information is hard to own because copying it is cheap; a research idea, once published or seen in a product, spreads to labs with more chips. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers.
positions.converts_if: A specialist's product becomes the tool a trade works in, so switching costs (what a customer would lose by moving to a rival) hold customers after the general labs catch up; or its data from customers and experiments passes Hagiu and Wright's tests and becomes a cornered resource, Helmer's term for preferential access to something others need. A general neolab converts only if its different route (a new way to train, or a model that learns after it is released) proves both better and hard to copy.
positions.kill_shot: A lab founded since 2023 taking the lead on general models and holding it while charging for it; or the specialists' niches being matched by the frontier labs' general models, with the specialists' prices falling to the general labs' level.
positions.mechanism: Neolabs are younger AI labs outside the big frontier group, most founded in the last few years and mostly funded by investors before they sell much: Mistral, which publishes the weights (the trained settings) of some of its models, Safe Superintelligence, Thinking Machines Lab, Reflection AI and Periodic Labs among the general and research labs; ElevenLabs, Black Forest Labs and others in voice, images and video; Physical Intelligence and Skild AI in robots. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. For a new lab the scarce input is its researchers and its bet on a route the big labs are not taking. This site judges that where that route leads somewhere the frontier labs are heading anyway, the new lab competes with them for chips and money on worse terms, and its people are worth more to a big lab than its business is to investors.
positions.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is the small number of researchers who can lead a frontier training run (the training of the most capable model of its time), and in the specialties, the data and tuning for one kind of work (a voice, a robot's movements, a laboratory's experiments) that general labs have not collected. Andrei Hagiu and Julian Wright, economists who asked when learning from customers' data keeps rivals out, found it does so only when the data is proprietary, keeps its value and improves the product for every customer; a specialty that passes those tests may hold. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier; this site finds no such power proven in the neolabs today.
positions.title: A new lab earns a rent only where its specialty lies off the big labs' path; elsewhere its asset is its people

positions.case: These readings cover all open models, including Meta's and Mistral's, not only this group's. Open models trail the best closed ones by [fact:open_lag] on this site's latest reading, and on OpenRouter, a service that routes developers' requests to many models, they took [fact:open_share] of the tokens among its most used models, though OpenRouter's users lean towards cheap models and firms that buy from the labs directly never appear there. This site reads the open models' gap to the closed frontier on Epoch's capability index (a score from Epoch, a research group that tracks AI, combining many tests of what a model can do) as unclear: it moves both ways between readings. The labs' finances differ: for MiniMax and Zhipu, a year of revenue at the current pace now exceeds what they raised in their share listings, the only rounds this site records for them; for DeepSeek it is far below.
positions.commoditising: The open model is a commodity by design: many hosts serve the same weights and compete on price, so the price of running it falls towards the cost of the chips and power. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers as lower prices and better products. This site judges open-weight labs are the clearest case of it in AI: the buyers and the hosts keep most of what the model is worth.
positions.converts_if: An open-weight lab's parent earns what the lab gives away: a cloud whose customers come for the free model and stay for the services, which David Teece, an economist who studied why inventors often fail to keep the returns from what they invent, would call owning the complementary assets (the hosting, sales and systems a product needs to reach buyers). Or giving the model away becomes counter-positioning in Helmer's sense, a model a closed lab cannot copy without cutting into its own paid business, with the parent collecting the reward.
positions.kill_shot: Closed labs keeping their prices on models that open ones already match, with open models' share of use falling; or an open-weight lab earning a lasting profit on the model itself rather than on hosting, services or a parent.
positions.mechanism: An open-weight lab publishes its model's weights, the trained settings that are the model, so anyone can run it on their own chips or rent it from a host. This site's open-weight labs include DeepSeek, Alibaba's Qwen team, Moonshot, MiniMax, Zhipu and StepFun, all of them Chinese; Meta's Llama models are open too, though this site counts Meta among the frontier labs and Mistral among the new labs. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off.
