A model anyone can copy is not scarce, so the lab that publishes it collects little rent on it; this site judges that it earns instead through hosting its own model, selling a better closed version, or serving a parent company or state that wants the model to exist.
positions.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is the skill to train a model near the frontier on fewer chips, which some of these labs have shown, and the chips themselves, which export rules make harder for Chinese labs to buy. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier; this site finds none proven for the open-weight labs, because a skill that shows up in a published model can be studied and copied.
positions.title: Open-weight labs give the model away, so they keep little of its value but cap what the closed labs can charge

positions.case: Demand has risen fast on the readings this site holds, all of them company posts or press reports rather than audited figures. Mercor's reported yearly revenue pace, counted before what it pays out to its experts, grew sharply between the start of 2026 and June, and this site reads the expert-data market as emerging; Surge AI was reported to have passed [fact:surge_revenue] of yearly revenue for 2024 without raising outside money. Handshake says that in 2024 the labs wanted qualified experts at scale, that finding and managing them was slow and scattered, and that talent became the bottleneck, and that its long ties with universities spare it the heavy recruiting spending its rivals bear. The labs are pulling the layer closer. Meta bought a minority of Scale AI's shares without votes in June 2025; its filing says it has no significant influence over Scale, but Scale's founder moved to Meta and the two widened their commercial ties. At the time, Scale counted Google, Microsoft and OpenAI among its customers. Scale now says its data underpins work at many of the leading labs, and that it has added large businesses and more government work. Mercor agreed in July 2026 to buy Deeptune, a maker of practice tasks for training, and said the pair would serve companies deploying AI agents (programs that carry out several steps of a task on their own) as well as labs. The leading sellers now offer ordinary companies evaluation (testing an AI system on the firm's own work), post-training (further training of a finished model on narrower material), and help putting systems to work and keeping them running; all of it is on their own pages, not in any filing. Mercor launched an enterprise product in March 2026 that it says maps how a firm's staff do their work, turns that into tests and rules for the firm's agents, and checks their output as they run. Surge AI's enterprise page offers to build tests around a firm's own work, compare models on quality, cost and speed, watch them once live and, where that is not enough, design a training programme and build its data. Scale AI's page says it builds, deploys and runs AI systems for businesses in fields such as energy, insurance and health. Handshake's page says it builds agents inside a client's own systems, lowers what they cost to run and trains models the client owns; in July 2026 it wrote that its tests let a firm find which work can move to cheaper models, among them open-weight ones (models whose trained settings are published so anyone can run them). None of them says how much of its revenue comes from these buyers. Whether expert data is actually short, this site cannot say: nobody publishes its prices or how long buyers wait, so the training-data input carries no tightness reading, and this site's tally of sellers naming labs as customers rises and falls with what sellers choose to disclose.
positions.commoditising: This site judges that ordinary labelling, the tagging of pictures and text on which the first data firms were built, is a commodity: many sellers, interchangeable work, and prices set by the pay of the workers. Andrei Hagiu and Julian Wright, economists who asked when learning from customers' data keeps rivals out, found it does so only when the data is proprietary, keeps its value, and improves the product for every customer. For the seller, expert data made to one lab's order fails the first and last of those tests, since the lab owns it and it helps only that lab, and it goes stale as each new model masters what it taught.
positions.converts_if: A seller's graded records, pooled across many buyers, become what Helmer calls a cornered resource (preferential access to something others need), such as checked outcomes of expert work that improve every buyer's model; or a seller becomes so built into a lab's training that switching costs (what a customer would lose by moving to a rival) hold it. Coase and Williamson would expect the labs to bring such work inside as it becomes specific to them. Meta's stake in Scale AI is the largest step towards it this site records, but it stops short: the stake carries no votes, and Meta's filing says it gives Meta no significant influence over Scale. The move to ordinary companies is a second route: if tests and graded records built for one firm improve the service for the next, they pass the tests of Hagiu and Wright and would compound; if each job stays made to one client's order, the sellers have swapped a few lab buyers for many consulting clients, paid for their people's time, and the rent stays thin.
positions.kill_shot: A seller keeping or widening its margin (what it keeps from each sale after paying its costs) as more sellers enter and the labs hire experts directly, because something it owns, a pool of experts no rival can reach or a record of graded work, grows more valuable with every lab it serves; or a seller earning a lasting margin from ordinary companies on tests and graded records that carry from one client to the next, which would show the rent outlasting the labs' need for people.
positions.mechanism: Human-data sellers such as Scale AI, Surge AI, Mercor, Handshake, Turing and Invisible find experts (doctors, lawyers, programmers, scientists), pay them to write questions and answers, grade a model's attempts and set down how they do their work, and sell the result to the AI labs to train on. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. This site judges that the scarce input here is expert time, found quickly and checked well, and that the seller is a broker of it: the work is made to one lab's order and becomes that lab's to keep. Kenneth Arrow, an economist who studied how markets handle knowledge, argued that information is hard to own because copying it is cheap; here the buyer, not the seller, ends up owning it. The leading sellers are now also selling downstream, to ordinary companies rather than labs. Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, and Oliver Williamson, an economist who studied contracts and found that whoever has built something useful to only one partner can be squeezed by that partner, explain why the labs pull this layer towards them. This site judges that the move to ordinary companies is the same logic run in reverse: a supplier integrating forward (taking on the next step of the work, closer to the final user) so that it is not at the mercy of a few concentrated buyers.
positions.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce, for now, is the ability to find, vet and pay many experts in a narrow field quickly, and to check their work well enough that a lab trusts it; Handshake's account of its university network and Mercor's stress on its talent network, matching and speed are both claims to that. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier. This site finds none proven here: the benefit of a large expert network is real, but experts can work for several sellers at once and the labs can hire them directly, so the barrier is not yet shown.
positions.title: Expert-data sellers broker a skill the labs cannot yet make for themselves; what they sell belongs to the buyer, so their rent lasts only while the labs need people

positions.case: This site counts the sellers from one public directory, which in July 2026 showed a small specialist market rather than a crowd; that count says the business exists, not whether it pays. Nobody publishes what environments cost or how long buyers wait, so the post-training input carries no tightness reading. The best sign for the makers is that larger firms are paying to own them. CoreWeave's filing says it bought OpenPipe, a platform for training AI agents by reinforcement learning, in September 2025, and soon after launched, with its Weights & Biases unit, a service that lets customers train this way without managing the machines. In July 2026 Mercor, a seller of expert data, agreed to buy Deeptune, an environment maker, and World Labs, a new lab, bought SceniX, a robotics firm this site files under environments. Buyers that pay to own makers, rather than rent their tasks, are judging that good environments and graders are worth having in-house. Against this unit, the rival view holds that models will set and grade their own practice, and a writer this site follows reports the labs turning from staged practice tasks towards records of real work inside firms; either would leave even expert-graded environments with little to sell.
positions.commoditising: This site judges that the practice ground itself, a copied website or a sandbox where code runs, is becoming a commodity: open-source tools and the clouds' own services supply it, and a lab can build one in-house. Andrei Hagiu and Julian Wright, economists who asked when learning from customers' data keeps rivals out, found it does so only when the data is proprietary, keeps its value, and improves the product for every customer. An environment built to one lab's order belongs to that lab, helps only that lab, and goes stale once models master its tasks, since a task every model passes teaches nothing.
positions.converts_if: A maker holds graders for a field every lab needs and cannot build, which Helmer calls a cornered resource (preferential access to something others need); or it collects graded outcomes from real work inside firms, which improve with every buyer and go stale slowly. Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, and Oliver Williamson, an economist who studied contracts and found that a buyer that depends on an asset built for it can be squeezed by whoever owns it, would expect the labs and compute firms to buy makers whose graders become specific to their training, as the buying so far suggests.
positions.kill_shot: Models learning long work whose results are hard to check from practice they set and grade themselves, so the labs stop buying expert-graded environments; or environment makers keeping a lasting margin (what it keeps from each sale after paying its costs) on tasks a machine can already grade.
positions.mechanism: Reinforcement learning trains a model by trial and error: it attempts a task, a grader (a program or a person that scores the attempt) marks it, and the model is nudged towards what scored well. An environment is the practice ground: a copy of a website, a codebase, a spreadsheet or a job, with tasks set inside it and a grader attached. Sellers such as Mechanize, Fleet, Halluminate, Matrices, Applied Compute and Plato build them for the labs. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. This site judges that building the practice ground is ordinary software work, so any rent sits in the grader: tasks whose right answer only an expert can judge are scarce, and tasks a machine can check are not.
positions.stays_scarce: This site judges that graders for work whose outcome is hard to judge, such as a legal filing, a clinical call or a long engineering job, stay scarce, together with the experts who can write them. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier; this site finds none proven among environment makers, whose tasks can be rebuilt by a buyer that has seen them.
positions.title: Practice tasks for training are made to order for a few labs; they hold value only where the grader checks work that is hard to check

positions.case: The clouds and serving firms already sell tuning beside the chips. Google's filing describes Vertex AI as a platform for tuning and deploying custom models and agents from many models, its own and others'; Nebius says its managed service lets companies tune open and custom models; Fireworks says its platform offers tuning, reinforcement learning and testing on top of serving; Baseten says its engineers work inside customers to post-train and serve their models. Compute firms and labs are buying the specialists: CoreWeave's filing records its purchase of OpenPipe, and this site's ledger records Anthropic buying Runhouse in April 2026 and Thinking Machines Lab taking on the Workshop Labs team the same month. Continual learning is young. The highest step this site has seen in production is a pipeline, described by its maker Trajectory, in which a newly trained add-on (an adapter, a thin layer of extra settings) can go live within about an hour; Baseten says it trains a small helper model on the fly from live traffic. Harvey says it worked with Fireworks to post-train its legal model by reinforcement learning in realistic legal work, which this site's ladder of continual learning files as research, not production. Models that keep folding a firm's knowledge into their weights as they work exist only in research. Nobody publishes what post-training costs, so this input carries no tightness reading.
positions.commoditising: This site judges that a one-off tuning of an open model on a firm's examples is becoming a commodity: open-source tools such as Unsloth do it for free, the clouds and serving firms bundle it, and each new general model narrows the gain. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers as lower prices and better products.
positions.converts_if: Continual learning works in production at scale, so a model that has learned a firm's work for months is costly to replace: switching costs in Helmer's sense (what a customer would lose by moving to a rival) for whoever runs it. Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, would add that the rent then goes to whoever holds that model, a cloud, a lab, a serving firm or the customer itself, and not necessarily to the firm that did the tuning.
positions.kill_shot: Independent tuning firms keeping their margins while the clouds and serving firms bundle tuning with the chips; or, the other way, each new general model wiping out the gains from tuning so firms stop paying for it at all.
positions.mechanism: Post-training is everything done to a model after its first, general training, changing its weights (the settings, fixed in training, that hold what the model has learned): tuning it on a firm's own examples, training it by trial and error against graders, and, in its newest form, continual learning, in which the model keeps updating as it is used. Sellers include Thinking Machines Lab, Prime Intellect, Adaptive ML, Predibase, Arcee, Unsloth, Trajectory and Baseten. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. Oliver Williamson, an economist who studied contracts, found that an asset built for one buyer, worth far less anywhere else, ties that buyer to whoever holds it. This site judges that a model tuned to one firm's work is such an asset, but that the tuning itself is a service anyone with chips and open tools (software published for anyone to use and change for free) can offer.
positions.stays_scarce: This site judges that the skill to run reinforcement learning at scale without damaging what the model already knew, and the record of a customer's own work that a continually learning model feeds on, stay scarce. On the tests of Andrei Hagiu and Julian Wright, economists who asked when learning from customers' data keeps rivals out, a customer's record helps only that customer, so it does not compound across customers; but it is specific in Williamson's sense. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier; this site finds none proven among the tuning firms today.
positions.title: Tuning a model for one customer is becoming a feature of the clouds and the serving firms; a rent survives only where the tuned model keeps learning inside the customer's work

positions.case: This site has no reading of this market's size or prices: it holds no revenue for any seller here, and the training-data input carries no tightness reading. The one move it records is NVIDIA's purchase of Gretel in April 2025, a chip maker taking a data generator in-house. This site judges that the cost of generating falls with the price of running models, which this site reads as easing. A paper this site watches is titled as a study of how generated data can make AI agents (models that carry out tasks by using software tools) forget how to find skills they had learned; this site has read only the title. The best case for a stand-alone seller, in this site's judgement, is privacy: sellers such as Tonic and Mostly AI make made-up copies of real records that banks, hospitals and other regulated firms can use without exposing real people's details, a need a lab's general model does not meet by itself. This site judges that need real but holds no reading of what it earns. No writer this site tracks argues that stand-alone generators win, so this unit names no rival view.
positions.commoditising: This site judges that generation itself is a commodity whose cost follows the price of running models down. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers as lower prices and better products. David Teece, an economist who studied why the firm that invents something often fails to keep the returns, called the inputs a product needs to reach its customers complementary assets; this site judges that the model and the chips a generator needs are held by the labs and chip makers, not by the generator.
positions.converts_if: A generator becomes the kind of copy a regulator accepts in place of real records, such as privacy-safe versions of health or bank data, turning its rent into a regulated one; or its way of checking generated data proves hard to learn, which Helmer calls process power (a way of working that takes rivals years to learn). Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, and Oliver Williamson, an economist who studied contracts and found that a buyer that depends on an asset built for it can be squeezed by whoever owns it, would otherwise expect the owners of models and chips to keep generation inside, as NVIDIA did.
positions.kill_shot: An independent seller of generated data keeping a lasting margin (what it keeps from each sale after paying its costs) while the labs' own models generate data ever more cheaply; or the labs paying more for generated data than for data from people in the same field.
positions.mechanism: Synthetic data is training data that a model or a program generates: made-up records that mimic real ones, worked problems with their answers, rewritten or translated text. Sellers include Datology, Tonic, Mostly AI, Rendered.ai and Synthesis AI; Gretel was one until NVIDIA bought it in 2025. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. Kenneth Arrow, an economist who studied how markets handle knowledge, argued that information is hard to own because copying it is cheap. This site judges that generated data is the plainest case of both: its inputs are a model and computing, which the labs and chip makers already own, so a separate seller has little scarce to charge for, unless it starts from data or a way of checking that others lack.
positions.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is the check: generated data is only as good as the test of whether it is right. Where a program can check, as when code runs or a proof holds, generated practice is abundant; where it cannot, people must check it, and that scarcity sits with the expert-data sellers and environment makers, not here. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier; this site finds none proven among the generators.
positions.title: Generated data is a feature of whoever owns the model and the chips, not a business of its own

positions.case: This site holds no reading of licence prices or of how much AI companies pay content owners, and the training-data input carries no tightness reading. It records Cloudflare, which stands between many websites and their visitors, buying Human Native, an AI data marketplace, in January 2026, and its outlook records Cloudflare counting most AI companies' crawlers taking far more pages than they send visitors back. A writer this site follows reports a lab buying an airline's records and data sellers buying those of start-ups that have wound down, which fits the judgement that records of real work, which no one else holds, are what sell. Against this unit, the rival view holds that AI companies will pay for what they read far more widely than for unique archives, and reads Cloudflare's purchase as a step towards a system in which AI developers pay for the content they train on. From the other side, if AI companies can train on public, generated or scraped material instead, even unique archives have little to charge for.
positions.commoditising: This site judges that ordinary web text is already a commodity for training: it has been read, copied into many open collections, and cannot be taken back. Kenneth Arrow, an economist who studied how markets handle knowledge, argued that information is hard to own because copying it is cheap. Andrei Hagiu and Julian Wright, economists who asked when data keeps rivals out, found it does so only when it is proprietary, keeps its value and is hard to copy; an archive sold to many labs fails the first test, and old text fails the second once it is in the models.
positions.converts_if: Courts or lawmakers settle that training on content needs the owner's permission, turning the owners' rent into a regulated one; or a licensing standard such as RSL becomes what AI crawlers must honour, which could give the brokers network economies in Helmer's sense (each publisher and each AI buyer that joins makes the market more useful to the others). Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, would expect the largest buyers to strike direct deals with the largest archives and leave the brokers the long tail.
positions.kill_shot: Owners of large, still-growing archives failing to win lasting payments because AI companies train on public, generated or scraped material instead; or ordinary web pages fetching licence prices as high as unique archives do.
positions.mechanism: Data licensing is AI companies paying the owners of text, images, audio or records for the right to train on them or to show them in answers. The middlemen this site tracks include TollBit and ProRata, which charge AI companies for reading publishers' pages; Protege, Created by Humans, Defined.ai and Human Native, which broker datasets; and the RSL Collective, which backs a standard way for sites to state their licence terms to AI crawlers (the programs that read websites for AI companies). David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. This site judges that an archive sold once becomes, in effect, part of every model trained on it, while content that keeps coming, such as a forum where people keep writing or a daily news service, can be sold again each year.
positions.stays_scarce: This site judges that archives which are unique, legally clean and still growing stay scarce: a platform's ongoing conversations, a publisher's daily reporting, a firm's records of how its experts work. The power belongs to the owners of those archives, most of whom sit outside this layer; the brokers in it earn a fee. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier; this site finds none proven for the brokers today.
positions.title: Licensed content earns a rent only for archives no one else holds that keep growing; the rest is priced near what it costs to copy

positions.case: The buying runs one way. CoreWeave's filing says it bought Weights & Biases in 2025, whose tools developers use to build, evaluate, deploy and monitor models and agents; that the unit's results were not material to CoreWeave's; and that the premium it paid over the value of the assets was put down mainly to the team and the expected gains from combining the two. The Humanloop team joined Anthropic in August 2025. OpenAI took on the founders of Context.ai in April 2025, bought Promptfoo, which attacks models to find security flaws, in March 2026, and agreed in December 2025 to buy neptune.ai, which tracks how models train. Fireworks, a serving firm, offers testing on its own platform beside tuning and serving. On the other side, the ledger this site keeps of signs that checking AI's work is sold as a category of its own records [fact:evals_ledger] such events so far. Nobody publishes whether good testing is in short supply, so this input carries no tightness reading.
positions.commoditising: This site judges that testing tools, the logging, the scoring against a set of questions and the dashboards, are becoming a commodity: open-source versions exist and the platforms bundle them. Public benchmarks (standard published tests used to compare models) go stale: once a test is published, models are trained towards it. Kenneth Arrow, an economist who studied how markets handle knowledge, argued that information is hard to own because copying it is cheap, and a published test is information.
positions.converts_if: Regulators or insurers require an outside tester's sign-off before AI is used in some kinds of work, turning the tester's rent into a regulated one; or one tester's name becomes the mark buyers insist on, which Helmer calls branding. Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, and Oliver Williamson, an economist who studied contracts and found that a buyer that depends on an asset built for it can be squeezed by whoever owns it, would otherwise expect the labs and clouds to keep buying testers whose tools become specific to their models, as they have so far.
positions.kill_shot: Independent testers growing faster than the labs' and clouds' own testing tools and keeping their margins (what they keep from each sale after paying their costs) as the platforms give testing away.
positions.mechanism: Evaluation firms test what a model or an agent can do and watch it once it is running, which the industry calls observability: logging what it did and flagging its mistakes. They include Braintrust, LangSmith (from LangChain), Arize, Galileo, Patronus, Vals AI, Confident AI, Atla, and LMArena, which ranks models by public votes. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. This site judges that testing tools sit close to the models and chips they test, so the firms that sell those can give testing away as a feature; what a buyer cannot get from the seller is a verdict from someone who is not the seller.
positions.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is a verdict the buyer trusts because the tester does not sell the model: tests for regulated work, for insurers and for buyers choosing between labs, built on private tasks no model has been trained on. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier; the one that would fit here is branding (buyers paying more for the same thing because of who made it), and this site does not find it proven for any tester yet.
positions.title: Testing AI is being folded into the labs' and clouds' platforms; an independent tester keeps a rent only where buyers need a judge who is not the seller

positions.case: Prices are falling: this site reads the running-models input as easing, from the price of the cheapest flagship model on OpenRouter, a marketplace that routes developers' requests to many models. Open models, which any host can serve, took [fact:open_share] of the tokens among OpenRouter's most used models, though its users lean towards cheap models. Nebius's filing names Fireworks and Together as rivals to its own managed service, which runs all the major open models and lets customers bring their own, and warns that larger rivals may cut prices or bundle. The serving firms describe a way out: Fireworks says nearly all the tokens it serves come from models specialised on customers' own data, and Baseten says its engineers work inside customers to tune and serve their models; both grew revenue sharply and raised large rounds in 2026. Chip and cloud owners are buying serving firms: Nebius agreed in May 2026 to buy Eigen AI and that month took Clarifai's technology and leaders; Nscale agreed in July 2026 to buy Anyscale; Crusoe bought Atero in August 2025; AMD bought Brium in June 2025 and has since bought or taken on other firms that speed up serving; d-Matrix bought Wallaroo.ai in August 2026; and the model labs Mistral and Zhipu agreed in February and June 2026 to buy serving firms. This site holds these firms' reported revenue paces but does not yet publish a reading for the layer.
positions.commoditising: This site judges that an answer from a published model is becoming a commodity: the same good from many hosts, with the clouds, the neoclouds (newer cloud firms built to rent out AI chips) and the chip makers all offering it. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers as lower prices. David Teece, an economist who studied why the firm that invents something often fails to keep the returns, called the inputs a product needs to reach its customers complementary assets; the chips and powered buildings a serving firm needs are owned mostly by others, which is why their owners can absorb the software on top.
positions.converts_if: A host keeps its customers' tuned models, and the loop of data that improves them, so moving to a rival means rebuilding the model: switching costs in Helmer's sense (what a customer would lose by moving to a rival). That route holds only if a tuned model keeps beating each new general model. Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, and Oliver Williamson, an economist who studied contracts and found that a buyer that depends on an asset built for it can be squeezed by whoever owns it, would otherwise expect the owners of chips and clouds to keep buying the serving software, as they are.
positions.kill_shot: Hosts of the same open model keeping different prices for long, with buyers staying with the dearer one; or serving firms keeping or widening their margins (what they keep from each sale after paying their costs) while chip rents fall and more hosts offer the same models.
positions.mechanism: Inference is running a trained model to answer requests. Serving firms such as Fireworks, Baseten, Together, Modal, Replicate, RunPod, DeepInfra and Hyperbolic rent or buy chips, load open-weight models (whose trained settings, the weights, are published) or a customer's own model, and sell the answers by the token (a fragment of a word) or by the hour of chip time. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. This site judges that serving a published model is close to a commodity, since many hosts offer the same model and compete on price towards the cost of chips and power; what a host adds is software that makes each chip answer faster and cheaper, which rivals learn.
positions.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is the engineering to run each new model fast on each new chip, and, for hosts that tune and run a customer's own model, the position of holding that model. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier. The likeliest here is scale economies (pooling many customers' uneven demand keeps shared chips busy, and a rival must match the volume to match the cost), but the chip and cloud owners can pool as well, so this site does not count it proven.
positions.title: Serving a published model is a price-taking business on rented chips; the serving firms are escaping into running each customer's own tuned model, and the chip and cloud owners are buying them

positions.case: Developers on OpenRouter spread their tokens (the fragments of words that models read and write, by which use is billed) across many models: this site's first readings of how concentrated its traffic is show no single model dominating, though too few weeks have passed to read a direction, and open models took [fact:open_share] of the tokens among its most used models. Stripe's agreement in August 2026 to buy OpenRouter puts what Stripe calls a leading AI model gateway inside a payments firm, which fits the judgement that its value lies in the bill as much as in the choice. The clouds offer their own catalogues: Google's filing describes a platform with many models, its own, other firms' and open ones. This site cannot measure how much a router saves, because the spread of list prices is set almost entirely by one very expensive model, so its routing gauge carries no reading. The router positions this site records disagree on whether pooling many firms' outcomes makes a router choose better than any one firm can.
positions.commoditising: This site judges that picking a model for each request is becoming a commodity: open-source gateways do it, the clouds' catalogues do it, and the labs' own tools do it for their models. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers.
positions.converts_if: Pooling many firms' checked outcomes lets a router choose better than any firm alone, a network economy in Helmer's sense; or, inside Stripe, the marketplace becomes where AI agents themselves pay for models, so billing and credit create switching costs (what a customer would lose by moving to a rival).
positions.kill_shot: Routers charging more for the choice of model itself, and buyers paying it, because choices learned from many firms' outcomes beat what each firm manages alone.
positions.mechanism: A router or gateway sits between an app and the models: it sends each request to a model chosen for price, speed or quality, switches when one fails, and keeps one bill. OpenRouter, which the payments company Stripe agreed in August 2026 to buy, sells access to many models through one account; Martian and Not Diamond sell the choice of model; Portkey, Helicone, LiteLLM and TrueFoundry sell a gateway a firm runs itself, LiteLLM's as open source (code published for anyone to use and change for free). David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. This site judges that the routing itself is easy to copy, while a marketplace that many developers and many model sellers both use can hold them the way a payments network does.
positions.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is the marketplace itself: one account, one bill and one set of terms across many model sellers, and the record of what traffic went where. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier. Network economies (each user makes the product more valuable to the others) would fit a marketplace, but developers use several routers or go straight to the labs, so this site does not count the barrier proven.
positions.title: Choosing a model is being given away; a gateway keeps a rent only as the place where developers pay for many models

positions.case: The clouds sell agent building as part of their platforms: Microsoft's filing describes Azure AI Foundry as a platform to design, customise and manage AI applications and agents, Google's describes Vertex AI as one for building agents as well as models, and CoreWeave's describes its own agent-building tools. The labs and clouds are also buying the plumbing: Nebius agreed in February 2026 to buy Tavily, which gives agents web search; OpenAI took on the Cirrus Labs team in April 2026 and agreed in June 2026 to buy Ona, which gives agents secure cloud workspaces; Anthropic agreed in May 2026 to buy Stainless, which makes toolkits and servers for connecting models to other software; Meta took in Moltbook in March 2026 and Stilla in September 2026. Platforms are deciding whether to let outside agents in: this site's ledger of big platforms fencing out agents that are not their own records [fact:fences_ledger] such events so far. This site reads agents' ability as easing, meaning the length of task they can finish keeps growing fast; that gauge measures agents, not the economics of their plumbing, for which this site has no reading.
positions.commoditising: This site judges that frameworks, sandboxes and simple memory are becoming commodities: most began as open source, the clouds bundle them, and the labs buy the teams that build them. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers. David Teece, an economist who studied why the firm that invents something often fails to keep the returns, called the inputs a product needs to reach its customers complementary assets; a generic one, which anyone can supply, earns an ordinary return, not a rent.
positions.converts_if: A connector firm becomes the standard way agents are given permission into business software across many firms, which could give it network economies in Helmer's sense (each user makes the product more valuable to the others), or its links into each customer's systems become switching costs. Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, would otherwise expect the labs and clouds to keep absorbing this layer, as the buying so far suggests.
positions.kill_shot: An open-source framework or sandbox firm earning a lasting margin (what it keeps from each sale after paying its costs) while the labs and clouds give the same thing away; or connector firms losing customers as fast as framework firms once the labs and clouds ship their own connectors.
positions.mechanism: An agent is a model that carries out a task by using software tools over minutes or hours. Agent infrastructure is what it needs, much of it open source (code published for anyone to use and change for free): frameworks for wiring model calls together (LangChain, CrewAI, Mastra), sandboxes where it can run code or a browser safely (Daytona, Browserbase and others), memory that lasts between sessions (Letta), and connectors that let it log in to and act in other software (Composio, Arcade, Nango, Merge). David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. Oliver Williamson, an economist who studied contracts, found that an asset built for one buyer, worth far less anywhere else, ties that buyer to whoever holds it. This site judges that frameworks and sandboxes are generic, while connectors that hold a firm's permissions and links into its systems are specific to that firm, and harder to replace.
positions.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is the working link into a firm's own software: the permissions, the audit trail and the map of which system holds what. That context helps only the firm it came from, so it does not compound across customers, but it is specific in Williamson's sense. The software that keeps a firm's records can also refuse or charge for outside agents, which is where the rival view places the rent. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier; switching costs (what a customer would lose by moving to a rival) are the likeliest here, but this site does not count them proven for any connector firm yet.
positions.title: Agent plumbing is mostly open source that labs and clouds buy or copy; the rent sits with whoever holds the connections into customers' systems

positions.case: Palantir's filing describes the route from services to software. It sells platforms that connect a customer's data and operations to large language models (the kind of AI model that reads and writes text) made by other firms; its software engineers working with existing customers run deployments and look for new uses; and it runs short workshops, which it calls bootcamps, that build working tools on a customer's own data within days. It also warns that pilots (trial projects) given at little or no cost may never turn into paying contracts. Much of its revenue comes from existing customers widening their use, and the average revenue from its largest customers rose in 2025 over 2024. No single customer reached the size at which the filing must report it in any year from 2023 to 2025, though governments bring in much of its revenue, and it names large software firms, government contractors and systems integrators (firms that assemble other companies' technology for a client) among its rivals. The labs are buying this layer: this site's record of acquisitions shows OpenAI agreeing to buy Tomoro as it launched the Deployment Company, and the Deployment Company agreeing to buy Northslope, both consultancies that put AI to work in large firms; and Poolside, a lab, buying Fern Labs, a deployment firm. This site's records also hold the Anthropic venture buying Fractional AI and Casper Studios, firms that build AI systems for clients; the record of acquisitions leaves those two out of its count under its written rules, because no single buyer controls the venture. Whether the work pays off is unsettled: in one survey of large firms, most AI pilots built into their systems showed no measurable effect on profit, though another survey, which counts differently, finds many more reaching everyday use.
positions.commoditising: This site judges that generic integration, wiring a model to a firm's documents and common business software, is becoming a commodity: the clouds and labs ship connectors (links that let a model read and act in other software) and tools for building agents (AI programs that carry out tasks on their own), and each new model needs less hand-fitting. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers. David Teece, an economist who studied why the firm that invents something often fails to keep the returns, called the inputs a product needs to reach its customers complementary assets. This site judges that the deployer owns neither the model nor the customer's records, so on generic work it earns an ordinary services return.
positions.converts_if: A deployer's work ends in its own platform, which the customer's operations come to run on, so replacing it means rebuilding the work, not repointing it: switching costs in Helmer's sense. Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, and Williamson would add that a lab owning the deployer keeps its model inside that platform, which is why the labs are buying consultancies. The rent stays with services margins if the models learn to fit themselves to a firm's work.
positions.kill_shot: Deployment firms keeping or widening their margins while the models need less fitting with each release and the labs give deployment away to win model sales; or, the other way, deployment staff becoming easy to hire while customers still stay with the firm that first fitted their systems.
positions.mechanism: Deployment firms send engineers into a customer to connect AI models to its data, systems and daily work. The industry calls them forward-deployed engineers: staff who sit with the customer rather than at head office. This site judges Palantir the largest listed firm doing this work, though Palantir describes itself as selling software platforms. The labs have set up their own deployment arms, among them the OpenAI Deployment Company and a venture Anthropic formed with Blackstone and other investors (reports in this site's records differ on who the others are) to serve companies owned by private-equity firms (investment firms that buy whole companies); and consultancies sell the same work. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. This site judges that the scarce input here is people who understand both the models and the customer's business, and that selling their hours earns a wage-like margin, because each new customer needs more of them. Oliver Williamson, an economist who studied contracts, found that an asset built for one buyer, worth far less anywhere else, ties that buyer to whoever holds it. This site judges that the rent appears only when the deployment leaves behind such an asset: software and a map of the customer's data that its work comes to run on.
positions.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is engineers who can turn a firm's messy data and unwritten habits into working systems, and, once that is done, the map of the customer's data and operations that the system runs on. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier. Switching costs (what a customer would lose by moving to a rival) are the likeliest here, and Palantir's expanding customers fit them, but its filing reports expansion, not how many customers leave, so this site does not count the power proven. The rival view holds that these engineers are scarce enough to collect a scarcity rent themselves, not a wage-like margin.
positions.title: Fitting AI into a firm earns a services margin that grows with headcount; a rent lasts only where the deployer leaves behind software the customer runs its work on

positions.case: Coding agents hold large and fast-rising run-rates (a recent month's revenue scaled up to a year) in this site's records. Cursor's grew sharply between February and June 2026 on press reports citing people close to it; Cognition says its own grew sharply between May and September 2026; and Anthropic said, in announcing a funding round early in 2026, that Claude Code's had grown sharply since the year began. The last two are company figures, not audited ones. This site holds no comparable readings for OpenAI's Codex or for GitHub's tools, though its record of acquisitions shows the teams of small coding-tool firms joining OpenAI's Codex division in 2025 and 2026. The labs and their owners are buying in. SpaceX took an option in April 2026 to buy Cursor for its own shares, and Cursor says the purchase was completed in August. SpaceX's quarterly filing says that alongside the option it agreed to give Cursor computing capacity and to work with it on improving xAI's Grok models and developing new ones jointly; that August Cursor released a Grok model it says the two built together. Cursor says the deal gives it SpaceX's fleet of GPUs (the chips AI runs on) to train stronger models that cost less to run; it had said in late 2025 that its in-house models already wrote a great deal of code. Lovable says it draws on several models, matching each part of a job to the one best suited to it, and tunes open-source models (free code anyone may use and change) of its own. Cognition names large firms, NVIDIA and Citi among them, whose engineering teams use its agent. Google hired away Windsurf's leaders in July 2025 and Cognition agreed to buy the rest of the firm; this site's record of acquisitions also shows OpenAI and Anthropic hiring the teams of smaller coding-tool firms. Microsoft's filing describes GitHub as a platform where developers add AI and agent tools across the whole of building software. Each use costs an app the model's price, which a classic software firm does not pay: ICONIQ, an investment firm, puts the gross margin (sales minus the direct cost of making them, as a share of sales) of the AI products in its survey at [fact:ai_app_margin]. Whether the agents make developers faster is less clear than their revenue suggests: randomised trials (tests that compare groups assigned by chance) by METR, a research group, have not found developers working faster with AI tools, and METR calls the evidence from its newer trial weak.
positions.commoditising: This site judges that the agent's wrapper, the editor, the chat window and the loop that lets a model run and test code, is becoming a commodity: several sellers offer much the same, open-source versions exist, and the labs bundle their own with their models. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers as lower prices and better products. David Teece, an economist who studied why the firm that invents something often fails to keep the returns, found that the firm holding the scarce inputs a product needs usually keeps the profit; here the lab holds the model, the scarcest input.
positions.converts_if: An agent becomes the place a firm's software is planned, reviewed and run, holding its rules, permissions and history, so leaving means rebuilding how its engineers work: switching costs in Helmer's sense. Or its record of developers' corrections trains models of its own good enough to cut what it pays the labs. Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, would otherwise expect the owners of models to bring the agents inside, as SpaceX did with Cursor.
positions.kill_shot: An independent coding agent keeping its customers and its margin through a year in which the labs cut their own agents' prices and ship better models to everyone at once, with customers not moving to the labs' tools.
positions.mechanism: A coding agent is an AI tool that writes, edits and tests software, from suggesting the next line to carrying out a whole task on its own. The independent sellers include Cognition, Replit, Lovable, Factory and Augment. The labs and their owners sell their own: Anthropic's Claude Code, OpenAI's Codex, and Cursor, made by Anysphere, which SpaceX, the owner of the lab xAI, bought in 2026 and which now works with xAI on its Grok models; and Microsoft sells coding tools through GitHub, a site where developers keep and share code. This site judges that the independent agents mostly run on models bought from the labs, paying by the token (a fragment of a word), though some train models of their own. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. This site judges that the scarce input in a coding agent is the model underneath, which the labs own, so an independent agent keeps a rent only for what it adds: its editor (the program in which developers write and read code), its grip on a firm's code and habits, and its own models where it trains them.
positions.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is the best coding model at any moment, and, for an agent maker, the record of how developers accept, reject and correct its work, which could train its own models. Andrei Hagiu and Julian Wright, economists who asked when learning from customers' data keeps rivals out, found it does so only when the data is proprietary, keeps its value and improves the product for every customer; a record of accepted code may pass the first and last tests, but goes stale as models improve. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier. Switching costs (what a customer would lose by moving to a rival) are the candidate, but this site judges that a firm can try a rival agent alongside the one it has, and no seller publishes figures on customers leaving, so this site does not count them proven.
positions.title: Coding agents are among the fastest-growing AI apps, but the labs sell their own and a lab's owner now holds Cursor; an independent agent's margin is a lease on the labs' models

positions.case: Several of these firms report revenue rising fast. Harvey's co-founder said in September 2026 that its annual recurring revenue (what customers have signed up to pay in a year) had grown sharply since January; Legora's chief executive describes the same kind of rise; Decagon told a reporter in August 2026 that its revenue had crossed a large milestone, and a research firm estimates that its run-rate (a recent month's revenue scaled up to a year) rose sharply from the end of 2025; and a research firm estimates that OpenEvidence's run-rate rose sharply between the end of 2025 and July 2026. All of these are company, press or research-firm figures, not audited ones. The apps are building their own assets: Harvey said in September 2026 that it had released its first open-weight model (one whose trained settings are published) tuned for legal work, and that it aims to help law firms build AI they own. OpenEvidence has content partnerships with the New England Journal of Medicine, the Journal of the American Medical Association and the American Medical Association; it gave its research agent free to verified American clinicians in 2025, and it said in March 2026 that most practising American physicians use it every day. Menlo Ventures, a venture-capital firm (one that invests in young companies), found in its survey that start-ups took [fact:startup_app_share] of what American firms spent on AI apps, though the survey leaves out AI built into incumbents' existing software. The labs and platforms are moving into the same trades. Anthropic said early in 2026 that its Cowork product has plugins (add-ons that give its model the tools and instructions for one job) for roles such as sales, legal and finance, and that it had widened its reach into health care; Microsoft's filing describes a cloud business, once called Nuance Healthcare, that sells AI to the health care industry; and this site's record of acquisitions shows OpenAI buying Torch, a health-care technology start-up, in January 2026. The same record shows labs and platforms buying vertical apps: Mistral bought Emmi AI and agreed to buy Pimento, OpenAI bought Crixet, Microsoft bought Fintool and Amazon bought NLX. Where the work is regulated, rules slow everyone: a start-up, UpDoc, said in December 2025 that the Food and Drug Administration had given its diabetes app the first clearance for medical software using large language models that talk to patients, though the agency's own record of the clearance does not describe it that way. Harvey's own test of expert legal work found the best general models finishing few of its tasks end to end in May 2026, a vendor's test not yet repeated by anyone else.
positions.commoditising: This site judges that a vertical app that adds only prompts (the written instructions given to a model) and a trade's vocabulary to a general model is becoming a commodity, since each general release learns more trades at once. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers as lower prices and better products. Kenneth Arrow, an economist who studied how markets handle knowledge, argued that information is hard to own because copying it is cheap; a clever way of asking a model a legal question is information of that kind.
positions.converts_if: A vertical app becomes the system of record for its trade, the software that holds a firm's matters, patients or cases, so switching costs in Helmer's sense hold customers when the labs catch up; or a regulator's approval, or the trade's liability rules, make the app's checked record something a lab cannot simply match, turning its rent into a regulated one. Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, would otherwise expect the labs to keep buying the apps whose trades they want.
positions.kill_shot: Vertical apps' prices and margins falling each time the labs release a better general model, with customers switching to the labs' own specialist products; or, the other way, a vertical app keeping its customers and prices after a lab ships a rival product for the same trade.
positions.mechanism: Vertical AI apps are built for one trade: Harvey and Legora for lawyers, OpenEvidence, Abridge and Ambience for doctors, Hebbia and Rogo for finance, Sierra and Decagon for customer service. They buy models from the labs and wrap them in the forms, checks and records of one kind of work. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. David Teece, an economist who studied why the firm that invents something often fails to keep the returns, found that the profit often goes to whoever holds the complementary assets: the distribution, the trade's trust and the systems a product needs to reach its buyers. This site judges that a vertical app earns a rent only where it holds such assets that a lab cannot copy by training a better general model.
positions.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is the place in the trade's daily work (the tool a lawyer drafts in or a doctor's notes are written by), the trade's own records the app is allowed to see, licensed content the trade trusts, such as the medical journals OpenEvidence draws on, and approvals that only a regulator or a licensed professional can give. Andrei Hagiu and Julian Wright, economists who asked when learning from customers' data keeps rivals out, found it does so only when the data is proprietary, keeps its value and improves the product for every customer; much of a trade's data belongs to each client and helps only that client. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier. Switching costs (what a customer would lose by moving to a rival) and branding (buyers paying more because of the name) are the candidates, but these firms are young and publish no figures on customers leaving, so this site counts neither proven.
positions.title: A trade's own AI app keeps a rent where it holds the trade's workflow, records and approvals; where it only packages a general model, each lab release takes the margin

positions.case: The platforms are putting AI where their users already are. Meta's filing says Meta AI is available across its apps, as a stand-alone app, on its AI glasses and on the web, and that Meta earns substantially all its revenue from advertising. Google's filing says its Gemini model runs across Search and the Gemini app, and warns that as AI enters Search it may earn money differently than it has in the past. OpenAI reaches consumers through ChatGPT directly; its paying subscribers stand at [fact:paid_share] of its weekly users on this site's latest reading, two different counts, so this is not the share of users who pay. The owners of habits are buying small consumer apps: this site's record of acquisitions shows OpenAI buying Roi, Torch, Hiro Finance and NextSlide, Meta buying Manus and Limitless, and Amazon agreeing to buy Bee. Users are getting much of the value: Stanford's Digital Economy Lab estimated what American users would have to be paid to give up generative AI (AI that writes text or makes images on request), and its total rose sharply between the middle of 2025 and early 2026; the survey counts only Americans. This site holds no revenue readings for the companion apps. A wave of personal agents arrived in 2026. Meta says its Muse, launched in September 2026, runs in a sandbox of its own (a separate computer in Meta's cloud, walled off from other users, with its own web browser), books travel, fills in forms and buys things, checks with the user before it sends an email or makes a purchase, and pays through Link, a checkout service built by Stripe; Meta also says Muse is free for most uses with paid plans for more, and does not share users' conversations with Muse, or the data in their Muse workspace, with its ad systems. Instinct, a start-up whose users text it, and whose concierge feature makes phone calls for them, uses its own phone number and computer to carry out tasks, TechCrunch reported when it raised a new round in September 2026 from investors including Sequoia Capital, Benchmark and Coatue, a month after its previous one. Manus, whose makers describe it as a general-purpose agent for research and complex tasks, announced in December 2025 that it was joining Meta. Assistant Benchmark, a site that tests assistants people can text on the same published tasks, ranked Muse first and Instinct second in its tests as of September 2026; the site, created by David Pawlan, says it scored the assistants it tested after real use; it had tested only some of those it lists, so these are one site's results, not a survey of users.
positions.commoditising: This site judges that answering an everyday question is a commodity: many free assistants do it well enough, and the price to the user is zero. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to users as lower prices and better products. On his finding, the gap between what users would pay and what they are charged is the value they keep. The rival view holds that the labs are durable, high-margin businesses whose customers mostly do not switch, which would leave more of the value with the makers.
positions.converts_if: An assistant's memory of each user becomes costly to leave, turning a habit into switching costs in Helmer's sense (what a user would lose by moving to a rival); or assistants learn what people want to buy early enough that advertisers pay more to reach them than in search, turning attention into the kind of rent search earned. It fails to convert if memories become easy to carry from one assistant to another. A third route opens with agents that buy for their users: the agent becomes the place where payment happens, and its owner takes a fee on each purchase, a rent on the sale rather than on attention. That fails to convert if users can move their saved cards, logins and preferences to a rival agent easily, or if shops and payment firms such as Stripe keep the fee.
positions.kill_shot: A consumer AI app with no existing platform behind it, such as a personal agent like Instinct, taking a large, paying audience from Meta, Google and ChatGPT and holding it; or consumer AI firms' revenue growing as fast as the value users say they get.
positions.mechanism: Consumer AI is the assistants and apps people use for themselves: OpenAI's ChatGPT, Meta AI inside Meta's apps, Google's Gemini in its app and in Search, Perplexity's answer engine, and companion apps such as Character.AI and Replika, which act as a friend or partner. Many people use them free; some pay a subscription, and advertising may pay for the rest. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. This site judges that in consumer AI the scarce input is a user's habit, the app someone opens without thinking, and that it is held by firms that already own people's phones, feeds and searches, plus ChatGPT, which built one of its own. A newer kind of consumer AI, the personal agent (an assistant that carries out tasks for its user, such as booking, shopping, filling in forms and paying, rather than only answering), adds a second question beside the habit: who stands where the user pays.
positions.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is the user's attention and habit, the personal history an assistant builds up about each user, and the payment and advertising systems that turn attention into money. David Teece, an economist who studied why the firm that invents something often fails to keep the returns, called those inputs complementary assets; Meta and Google held theirs before AI arrived. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier. Network economies (each user makes the product more useful to the others) and scale economies hold in the platforms' existing businesses, but this site finds none proven for AI assistants themselves, where one user's chat does not make another's better and people use several at once. This site judges that agents which act, not just answer, could move both the habit and the point of payment: if people hand their errands to one agent, the firm running it stands between them and every shop they buy from, and could take a cut of each purchase, as card networks and app stores do, or charge sellers to be chosen. Whether that rent goes to the platforms that already own the habit, such as Meta with Muse and Manus, or to newcomers such as Instinct is open; one tester's early rankings are not evidence of lasting use. Because Meta says Muse keeps users' conversations with it, and the data in their Muse workspace, out of its ad systems, this site judges that, for now, the source suggests any money Muse makes would come from subscriptions or purchases rather than advertising.
positions.title: In consumer AI the rent goes to whoever owns the daily habit, and users keep most of the value

positions.case: This site holds no revenue or margin readings for any AI rollup; the evidence is structural. The site's automatability census, which screens tasks for whether their shape would let them be handed to software, asks of each trade whether its owner would keep the saving, and answers from how the trade sends its bills. Where the bill counts hours, as in most accounting and audit work, cutting the time cuts the bill and the client keeps the saving, which is why the census calls accounting its false positive. Where the fee is set by something other than the firm's own costs, such as a share of a placed candidate's salary, a commission on a booking or a fixed fee set by the payer, the owner can keep it until the price is next reset. The labs are reaching the same buyers another way: OpenAI has set up the OpenAI Deployment Company, which is buying consultancies that put AI to work in large firms, and Anthropic has formed a venture with Blackstone and other investors (reports in this site's records differ on who the others are) to serve companies that private-equity firms (investment firms that buy whole companies) own. This site's entry for General Catalyst's plan rests on a press report not yet confirmed by a second source.
positions.commoditising: This site judges that the AI a rollup uses is bought from the labs and software firms like any other customer's, so it gives no lasting edge over a rival firm that buys the same tools. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part; most goes to buyers. In a trade where clients re-bid their contracts, a saving becomes a lower price once rivals match it. The rival view holds that AI lets one centre see and run many unrelated businesses, an edge that would outlast the tools themselves.
positions.converts_if: A rollup turns its running of many firms into a way of working rivals take years to learn, what Helmer calls process power, or grows large enough in one trade and place that its costs per client fall below any single firm's, his scale economies. Both need the saving to outlast the next time clients re-bid, which in trades billed by the hour means moving clients to fixed fees first.
positions.kill_shot: AI rollups in trades billed by the hour keeping higher margins for years after buying, without moving clients to fixed fees; or rollups' margins falling back to their trades' ordinary level as rivals that did not merge buy the same AI tools.
positions.mechanism: A rollup buys many small firms in one trade, such as accounting, property management or home services, and runs them as one. The groups this site files as AI rollups, among them Thrive Holdings, Long Lake, Crete, Dwelly and Titan, and funds such as General Catalyst that have set money aside to build them, plan to run the firms they buy with AI and keep the saving. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, and Oliver Williamson, who studied contracts and found that whoever depends on an asset owned by someone else can be squeezed by its owner, would read a rollup as a bet that owning the customer, the licence and the trust is worth more than selling software to the firm that owns them. This site judges that the bet pays only where the firm's prices do not fall when its costs do.
positions.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce is the customer relationship, a licence or professional's signature where the trade needs one, and prices that are set by something other than the firm's costs. David Teece, an economist who studied why the firm that invents something often fails to keep the returns, called such inputs complementary assets and found that their owners often keep the profit; the rollup buys them rather than building them. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier; this site finds none proven for any AI rollup yet.
positions.title: A rollup keeps AI's saving only where the firms it buys are paid for results rather than hours; its asset is the customer, and the AI is bought in

positions.case: Use is spreading, but slowly and unevenly. The Census Bureau's survey of American businesses finds [fact:firms_using_ai] of firms using AI in their work. This site sets the normal range for that reading at the pace at which personal computers and online selling spread through firms, and the reading sits inside it. Ramp, a company that handles businesses' card spending and whose customers lean towards technology, puts the median (the middle firm's figure when all are ranked) AI spending per employee at [fact:ramp_spend], against [fact:ramp_spend_year_ago] a year before. Payoffs are hard to find so far: in a survey of executives published in early 2026, most said AI had made no measurable difference to their own firm, and in another survey of large firms most AI pilots (trial projects) built into their systems showed no measurable effect on profit. Studies of single jobs find real but modest gains, as in one study of customer-support staff using an AI assistant. Many workers in the jobs most exposed to AI (those whose tasks AI can most readily do, on researchers' measures) do not yet use it weekly, on the research this site follows. This site's automatability census asks, trade by trade, whether the owner would keep a saving, and finds the answer turns on how the trade sends its bills: by the hour, and the client keeps it; by a fee set elsewhere, and the firm can.
positions.commoditising: This site judges that AI itself is becoming a commodity to the adopting firm: the same tools are sold to it and to its rivals, and their price keeps falling. David Teece, an economist who studied why the firm that invents something often fails to keep the returns, found that generic inputs anyone can buy earn only an ordinary return; on his account a firm's advantage from AI lasts only as long as its rivals are slower to adopt it.
positions.converts_if: Early adopters rebuild their operations around AI in ways rivals take years to copy, process power in Helmer's sense; or they hold prices that are set by something other than their own costs, such as a share of what the client spends or a fee a regulator sets, so the saving stays with them. Ronald Coase, an economist who studied why some work is done inside firms rather than bought, would add that cheaper checking and contracting could also move work out of firms to AI-run suppliers, handing the saving to whoever runs them.
positions.kill_shot: Firms that adopt AI earning higher profits than rivals that do not for years after the tools became widely available, in trades where prices are set by competition; or the share of firms reporting a measurable payoff jumping as use spreads.
positions.mechanism: The adopters are the ordinary firms that buy and use AI, from banks and hospitals to shops and law practices. When AI cuts a firm's costs, the saving can go three ways: to the firm as profit, to its customers as lower prices, or to its workers as higher pay. David Ricardo, an English economist who asked in 1817 why landlords grew rich when bread grew dear, found that the owner of the scarcest input collects a rent: profit above what it takes to keep a business going, earned because something holds rivals off. William Nordhaus, an economist who measured how much of the value of new inventions their makers keep as profit, found that it is a small part and that competition passes most of it on as lower prices. This site judges that the same holds one step down: a firm that adopts AI keeps the saving only until its rivals adopt too, unless its prices are set by something other than its costs. For a layer of buyers, the direction word describes the AI they buy: commoditising means that input is getting cheaper and more alike from seller to seller, so its gains pass to the adopters, unless competition among them passes the gains on again to their own customers.
positions.stays_scarce: This site judges that what stays scarce, for the adopter, is the skill to rebuild its work around AI rather than add AI to old work, and its own records of how that work is done. Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant who studied why some firms keep earning more than their investors could expect elsewhere, found that a lasting advantage is a benefit behind a barrier; process power, a way of working that takes rivals years to learn, is the one that could fit an early adopter, but this site cannot yet see it in any reading.
positions.title: Firms that adopt AI keep its saving only where competition and their pricing let them; so far use is spreading at the pace of past technologies and few report a payoff

positions.case: On the consumer side, Stanford's Digital Economy Lab estimated what American users would have to be paid to give up generative AI (AI that writes text or makes images on request), and its total rose sharply between the middle of 2025 and early 2026. On the labour side, the readings are mixed and early. The jobs most exposed to AI are those whose tasks AI can most readily do, on researchers' measures. In those jobs, employment of workers in their early twenties has moved [fact:junior_gap] against older workers since late 2022, against [fact:junior_gap_control] in the least exposed jobs (a minus sign marks the young falling behind), in payroll records that move with anything that treats young and old differently.
